Sports.title: Doubts had been gathering about Roberto De Zerbi but not now, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI, as Crystal Palace's ludicrous acts of self-sabotage prove costly in 2-0 defeat
Sports.content:
For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham have won three games in succession. If that proves Roberto De Zerbi’s prowess over at least two of his predecessors, then he will presumably reserve some thanks to the assistance of Crystal Palace.

On a night when Palace crossed to the north of London, with their manager in grave danger of the sack, they contrived to commit an utterly ludicrous act of self-sabotage in two phases.

The first defined the match, with Jean-Philippe Mateta dismissed after only 13 minutes for a challenge that was as brainless as it was dangerous.

From there, Pierre Sage’s side quickly conceded from a set-piece with the sort of defending that explained why Palace have shipped more goals than any other team in the top flight. That no further damage was inflicted until Jan Paul van Hecke’s second-half header was less reflective of the game than the tally showing 34 Tottenham shots to Palace’s two.

Given Sage’s tenuous grip on his job, and the thunderous face in the crowd of his chairman, Steve Parish, that might prove to be the final straw. If it is, Mateta should at least have the decency to drive him to the airport.

Sage said: ‘I am responsible. I have to find solutions. They have to trust in me because I will give my life for it. If I have one hour or 10 years, I will try my best.’

Archie Gray opened the scoring for Tottenham after 25 minutes to settle the nerves

Jan Paul van Hecke slid in to make it 2-0 and all but wrap the game up for the home team

In the recent past, such doubts were gathering around De Zerbi, but not now, and especially with a favourable run of fixtures on the horizon. Having belatedly entered the top half of the table, his side are finally aligning results with performances, even if this fourth game in an unbeaten stretch was aided so much by the opposition.

There remains an issue with chance conversion – both Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush were underwhelming here, with the slight mitigation that Palace spent the better part of 75 minutes camped on the edge of their own area. Marmoush, who started at No 10 after earlier games on the left and up front, appears no closer to revealing his best position.

De Zerbi’s solution was to direct traffic to the wings and it worked a treat. Mathys Tel, riding the isolated high of his performance against Chelsea, was again sharp. So too Mohammed Kudus. But the real gains for Tottenham in this purple patch have come from the central pairing of Sandro Tonali and Matheus Fernandes.

They cost a fortune to acquire and have taken their sweet time to gel, but that partnership has developed to strong effect. On the ball, they are the tempo setters, and off it they have shaped the press that is key to De Zerbi’s system. They controlled this game.

‘Tonali was unbelievable,’ said De Zerbi. ‘We played with two players more - Tonali (counted) double.’

He added: ‘I am very happy with the performance. (But) if we want perfection we have to be more nasty. If I am No 9 or No 10 I want to score.’

The last sentence is very much the Tottenham riddle – an inability to finish what they start. But those frustrations are now coming from an upwardly mobile situation.

Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi is banishing the doubters as his team climb the table

Having belatedly entered the top half of the table, Spurs are finally aligning results with performances

For Sage, along with whatever consequences this result brings, the regret will come from knowing his side had looked decent out of the gate.

But the red card eradicated those traces of momentum. Initially, referee Michael Oliver felt a booking was sufficient for Mateta’s studs-up lunge into Micky van de Ven’s ankle, but the VAR suggested an upgrade. On review, Oliver agreed.

Sage’s reaction? He had a look of pure deflation. The tackle was bad enough but the need to make it was non-existent – Mateta was chasing a losing cause in Tottenham’s half against one of the quickest defenders in the league. Dismal.

Naturally, it shifted the game in Tottenham’s favour, if only to the effect of a one-goal lead by the break. As with Mateta’s dismissal, the Spurs breakthrough was avoidable for Palace, with Gray left unmarked at the far post before planting his head on Kudus’s high, looping corner.

The video analysis will do Sage no favours. Kudus’s delivery was excellent, that much is true, but five Tottenham men had gathered at the far post with only three markers – even factoring for the red card, the tracking of Gray was abysmal.

At half-time, De Zerbi substituted Gray, who was carrying a yellow card, and Spurs maintained momentum by creating openings for Tel, Matheus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Solanke.

Palace were being pummelled but survived until Van Hecke’s finish for 2-0. As with the Chelsea win, Fernandes stood out in its creation with an excellent cross, from which Van Hecke powered a header at Dean Henderson.

The initial save was good, but the ball returned to Van Hecke, who was sat on his backside and able to steer his second header past Henderson. Sage could use similar inspiration from the floor.

Sports.title: Angry Oliver Glasner fumes at 's*** situation' in explosive rant: Nottingham Forest boss warns players they need to change or he'll be sacked and hits out at 'pattern' of problems
Sports.content:
Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner launched into an extraordinary rant after his team's 2-0 defeat at Brentford on Saturday left them second to bottom of the Premier League.

And Glasner made it clear that if things don't improve he will be sacked, or even walk away from the City Ground job.

Daily Mail Sport understands the under-fire Austrian is not happy with some of his players' attitudes and their response to his work since joining the club from Crystal Palace in the summer.

Glasner revealed that he had refused a request from one of his players to make his own way back to Nottingham from London after the game, banging the table at the press conference when revealing his dismay at the very idea.

'We have to accept it's not good enough,' he said. 'If we lose four of the last five games, it's not good enough. And that's why for me, it's now time that we change things, that I change things, and that's what I will do.

'Everywhere, and I feel I could see a few things from day number one. I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it's always compromises.

Oliver Glasner made his feelings clear after the final whistle, with Forest in the bottom three

Striker Igor Thiago's goal secured the latest triumph for upwardly-mobile Brentford

'It's a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.

‘I have no consequences. I think you see that. For me, I go home and have breakfast with my family. It's not the worst situation. Nobody needs to have pity with Oliver Glasner or with the manager. If I want, I could start in two weeks somewhere else. I won't do it.

'But, you know, the players, the staff, they remain in the same situation. And it's the same, sorry for the word, s*** situation that the club had last year.

'So you need to change and rebuild from the bottom to the top. And this is clear for me. And this is what I will do. And without any compromises. Zero. Zero. And if these things don't work, they will let me know [about my exit].'

The Bees had taken the lead after half an hour when Nikola Milenkovic steered the ball past his own goalkeeper. Igor Thiago continued his return to form as his second-half strike helped Brentford end their five-game wait for a win against the Midlands side.

For Glasner, it was all too much. 'I didn't come to Nottingham because I was bored at home,' he went on. 'No, I came to Nottingham to succeed. I came to Nottingham to get the visions of the owner and the fans and the club to reality. And therefore we need to have a bigger change than maybe I thought, to be honest.

'But again, when you're in a club, then you see what's going on. And I'm desperate to get this tournament around.

'But again, Oliver Glasner can't do anything alone. And I said this so often, and not just after a defeat. I always said the same after winning.

'It's not me, no, but we're all together and can do it. But I know where we have to go. And therefore, it's exactly this, being ruthless. And either you buy in or you leave. It's the only way.

'There is no compromise. Either you buy in where we want to go as a club. Because, and I mentioned it, if you're three times struggling, four or five Premier League seasons, struggling, being at the bottom of the league, there is a pattern.

'And I just know that Oliver Glasner is not here for five years. You see my mood, right? So, yes (I understand fans’ boos).

'And again, that's what should be expected. They say, hey, yes, we are nice. I paid the train ticket and the ticket here.

'And then, yeah, we're the same again. I think it's not, again, it's not a lack of effort, but there are a few things very obvious. And it's, let's say, we're talking about the realities.

'We are outrun by the opposition in every single game to change it. And if you can't change it, we need different personnel. And if the club doesn't want to change it, they need a different manager. I'm desperate to change it. Desperate.'

Sports.title: Why you can't blame Aston Villa chiefs for fighting back at Jamie Carragher as Fulham refuse to follow pundit in backing down as they earn deserved point, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE
Sports.content:
Aston Villa might have had an apology from Jamie Carragher but Unai Emery’s men found Fulham far more awkward opponents on a difficult night at Villa Park.

After Villa had threatened legal action, the Sky Sports pundit said sorry for telling ‘Aston Villa fans’ to ‘shut the f*** up’ on Saturday. The Holte End let Carragher know what they thought of him within a minute here.

Unfortunately for Villa, Fulham were in no mood to back down as Carragher had. John McGinn missed a penalty for the home side early on and though Nicolas Jackson gave them a half-time lead, Fulham deservedly equalised when Zion Suzuki – outstanding until then – carried Alex Iwobi’s corner over his own line.

Though Villa were very poor in the second half, this remains a team in transition and there will be bumps in the road. And thanks to the dispute with Carragher, the main talking point on Saturday was away from the pitch.

Why did Villa take this step?

Villa have been mocked for this response but look at it from their point of view. The club feel that at every turn, the established order are trying to slow their progress.

Consider the financial regulations that favour historically wealthy clubs who make money off the pitch, over those who have started to succeed on it.

Nicolas Jackson has been on fire this season and netted again to give Villa the lead

Villa would certainly have settled for Champions League fixture pile-ups 10 years ago

Imagine the frustration of finishing fourth in the Premier League, winning the Europa League and then having to sell six starters from the Final.

Now he has to listen to ex-players with significant influence telling the world that Villa can never satisfy Emery’s ambition.

Carragher is probably guilty of nothing more than expressing an opinion, however crudely he may have done so. But if Sawiris is fed up of various voices and organisations trying to put Villa back in their box, who can blame him?

Impressive Fulham

Whenever Antonee Robinson charged down the Fulham left, Villa were in trouble. The US international had a superb match but until his error, the visitors found Suzuki in excellent form.

He made one outstanding stop from Oscar Bobb and produced decisive interventions to deny Gonzalo Garcia, Josh King and Alex Iwobi.

There is plenty of technical ability in this side and when they move forward they are great to watch. But Garcia does not look a ruthless finisher in the style of Jackson and he missed chances here. At the back, too, they look flimsy. As well as Jackson took his goal, the challenges from Timothy Castagne and David Affengruber were weak.

Yet in Josh King and Oscar Bobb they have twinkle-toed attackers capable of threatening any defence. After a poor start to his tenure, it looks as though Alvaro Arbeloa is starting to find his range at Craven Cottage and had they won here, it would have been fully merited.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki got into a terrible mess to gift Fulham an equaliser

No rest for the wicked

Villa would certainly have settled for Champions League fixture pile-ups ten years ago, when they were eking out a 1-1 draw at rivals Birmingham in the Championship, but their recent schedule has been unforgiving.

With Villa facing Barca at the Nou Camp on Tuesday, the Fulham game was brought forward from 2pm on Sunday to the late fixture on Saturday. That is exactly 72 hours after the Carabao Cup defeat to Bournemouth, and 72 before they face the Spanish champions.

Given Villa made several changes at Bournemouth, surely there was a case making this a 12.30pm kick-off, or even a 3pm kick-off on Saturday? Given the short turnaround before facing one of Europe’s strongest sides, Villa will be glad to have won their opening three games.

That gives them a clear shot at the last 16, either by qualifying directly or through the play-offs. Barcelona also opted not to rest players and fielded a strong side against Alaves in La Liga on Saturday, which was also an 8pm kick-off.

The bad news is that Hansi Flick’s side were 4-0 up at half-time and went on to win 6-1. If Fulham were able to cause Villa this much trouble with sharp passing and movement, what about the club most associated with those qualities?

Emery and his squad will certainly travel to Barcelona a little nervously on Monday afternoon.

Sports.title: Tottenham look set to deliver after so many disappointments but Roberto De Zerbi's side need a nasty streak if they are to build on their momentum ahead of a daunting festive period, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI
Sports.content:
Tottenham look set to deliver after so many disappointments but Roberto De Zerbi's side need a nasty streak if they are to build on their momentum ahead of a daunting festive period, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

It was late on Saturday evening when Roberto De Zerbi relayed a few of the comments he had shared with Tottenham’s players at half-time in their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace. One of those remarks was indicative of how quickly things can change.

In the knowledge that his side were 45 minutes away from a rare spot in the upper portion of the table, he reminded them: ‘We can't forget where we have been two weeks ago. Two weeks ago, before the Coventry game, we were last in the table and we can't forget.’

With Tottenham, it is always prudent to know calamity is never too far away, but for the first time in two years, there is a gathering excitement at the club - in the crowd and the dressing room.

The win over Palace was assisted hugely by Jean-Philippe Mateta’s red card after 13 minutes, but Spurs have an uncanny knack of slipping on the easier opportunities. Not this time – goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke punctuated a dominant performance and a third straight win. Three managers and 616 days had expired since the last such streak.

But Spurs appear to be on the march and a promising season is belatedly taking shape. To finally deliver after so many disappointments, there are certain areas where improvements must follow…

Roberto De Zerbi reminded his players of where they had come from during their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace

Time to get nasty…

That was De Zerbi’s own assessment of his frontline after a familiar shortcoming against Palace may have been concealed by the win. It was not lost on him that both of Tottenham’s goals were scored by defenders, nor that they had 34 shots to Palace’s two. As ever, Spurs had abundant creativity in their side but lacked a clinical edge.

De Zerbi said: ‘If we want to follow perfection, we have to be more nasty, no? That is an individual thing, because if I'm number nine, number 10, I want to score. But I can't say nothing.’

He later clarified that comment to encompass the whole side, but it was clear that the onus falls most on Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush.

In fairness to the pair, Palace defended so deep after Mateta’s dismissal that they had no space to operate, but one goal apiece this season is a poor return. Solanke, in particular, needs to do a better job of reading the movements and intentions of those around him – too often on Saturday he appeared a thought or two behind Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus, who both impressed in the more generous spaces out wide.

De Zerbi wants his side to develop a 'nasty' streak - particularly his attackers

Nail down a role for Marmoush

Marmoush is an interesting case for De Zerbi. His mobility and technical ability are clear but he is yet to reveal his best position. On Saturday he was used as a No 10, having already been switched between roles on the left and up front. This experiment drew muted results.

It might be the case that a sustained run in one spot would be beneficial, but for now there appears to be confusion over where to use him. There is also a nagging thought that his best striking potential comes in a two-striker system, as shown in his most prolific period at Frankfurt, but that is not the way De Zerbi plays.

Maintain the middle

A significant improvement for Tottenham has come in midfield and, specifically, the pairing between Matheus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali.

Acquired at great cost, there was limited patience around the delivery of their impact, but time was always necessary, because De Zerbi’s system is notoriously complicated. In recent weeks, Fernandes and Tonali have shown signs that the penny has dropped on what they have to do.

This has been especially relevant in the instance of Tonali, who is very much the tempo-setter of the side on the ball and off it. On Saturday, he was excellent, or worth ‘double’ in the words of De Zerbi. There were times earlier in the season when he appeared disinterested, as if Tottenham was not the destination he had in mind, but his work rate was brilliant against Palace – he covered 12.3km, won all three of his tackles, and completed 93 per cent of his passes. He was all-action.

The same would be said for Fernandes, who covered 11.6km of ground and finessed a superb cross for Van Hecke’s goal. As a pair with Tonali, he was key to the pressing operation that limited Palace to a single counter-attack in the second half.

Mateus Fernandes (pictured) and Sandro Tonali have been huge boosts in the midfield

Team dynamics

De Zerbi struck an interesting note after the game by alluding to the cohesiveness of his side and how it has changed on the pitch. Perhaps that relates to the recent team-bonding exercise in Marbella, but more likely they just needed time to understand the complexities of their manager’s demands.

‘I think even before the innational break we were playing well,’ De Zerbi said. ‘We were playing maybe not 90 minutes, but many parts of the game we played very well. We didn't score. We conceded a stupid goal and then we lost energy. We lost spirit. We lost the right union between the players.

‘If we compare Tottenham before the innational break and Tottenham after the innational break, now we are playing as a team. Before the innational break we were playing as many very good players, but not as a team.’

Archie Gray, for one, is getting to grips with the less familiar brief at right-back. The requirements to swap spots with Fernandes, overlap Kudus or hold the advanced position are mind-scrambling, but he has adapted well. His withdrawal at half-time against Palace was down to his first-half yellow card and doesn’t detract from a salient point – he can evidently be trusted to replace Pedro Porro, or at least give the latter scope for a breather.

Make hay

Tottenham have an opportunity now. Their next four fixtures are Leeds, Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, with a nasty run waiting in December and early January.

If they can get something from Elland Road, the other three assignments present a rich opportunity for momentum before the tricky festive period.

One key area to improve in the short term will come against defensive sides who offer less space. That Spurs scored only twice from 80 per cent possession against Palace highlighted the issue.

De Zerbi said: ‘We are improving in the principle and the quality of play. Maybe we are not ready yet to play against such a low block but maybe in two or three months we will be.’

Sports.title: After Robbie Fowler claimed the moon landing is 'bulls***' and dubious Joe Cole said he has 'questions' for Neil Armstrong... who makes our ultimate XI of football conspiracy theorists?
Sports.content:
Robbie Fowler certainly helped to draw attention to his new podcast with his former Liverpool and England team-mate Steve McManaman this week by airing his views on the 1969 moon landing. After answering fan questions ranging from favourite films, comedians and useless talents, Fowler responded to McManaman's prompt of the moon landing as a conspiracy theory. 'I think the moon landing is bulls*** to be fair,' with an excited McManaman declaring 'that is a massive one,' before declaring his subsequent reasoning made 'perfect sense'. He is far from the only footballer to have doubts, with another ex-England international Joe Cole declaring he would like to sit down with Neil Armstrong – who died in 2012 – to get to the bottom of it. Fowler later quipped he is 'not a flat earther' having been up on a plane. However, some former footballers are, while others have raised a wide range of conspiracies, ranging from the small scale to the more wild. Here, Daily Mail Sport puts together our ultimate XI of football's conspiracy theorists. Former Liverpool forward Robbie Fowler admitted this week he believes the moon landing is 'bulls***' Source: YouTube - We'll have a look podcast GK: David Icke For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist – so entrenched in his off-the-wall beliefs and so willing to share them publicly that he is more widely known as a crackpot than a goalkeeper. Nevertheless, Icke turned out for Coventry City's youth set-up between the sticks in the late 1960s, and later played for semi-professional outfit Hereford United before hanging up his boots and pivoting to sports journalism. While his playing career might have been small-fry, his commitment to conspiracy theories is Premier League. Among his often-cited beliefs is the idea that an inter-dimensional race of reptile-like shape-shifters – the 'Babylon Brotherhood' have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society. Among the accused are the late Queen Mother, the Rockefeller and Rothschild families, and former Prime Minister Edward Heath, whose eyes, Icke alleged, he saw turn 'jet black' when the pair met in 1989. Icke also believes that the 'Illuminati' at the top of the global food chain organised world events including Dunblane, 9/11, the assassination of John F Kennedy, the death of Princess Diana to prompt their subsequent responses. Less laughable is the thick seam of anti-Semitism which critics believe runs through his thinking, although Icke has denied this. For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist, with one of his cited beliefs is the idea that reptile-like shape-shifters have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society RB: Javi Poves Javi Poves endured a similarly unmemorable professional playing career in Spain, but did at least register one La Liga appearance with Sporting Gijon. Then, he quit. It was a matter of principle: he had grown to believe that 'professional football is only money and corruption'. Not an unreasonable view point, from some perspectives, but years on from his 2011 resignation things become somewhat more surreal. Poves joined lower-division Madrid club Mostoles Balompie in 2016 and later became the club's president. In 2019, he renamed the club Flat Earth FC, to draw attention to his primary cause. 'Football is the most popular sport and has the most impact worldwide, so creating a club dedicated to the flat earth movement is the best way to have a constant presence in the media,' he said that year. 'Flat Earth FC is the first football club whose followers are united by the most important thing, which is an idea.' Although Poves has since moved to fellow amateur side CDC Moscardo, he remains passionately committed to the idea that the earth is flat and not round, and other environmentally-rooted conspiracy theories. These include viewing 'chemtrails' as a deployment of toxic chemicals, and refusing to believe that suncream can help prevent skin cancer. CB: Dejan Lovren One thread which runs through a number of players included in the XI is a scepticism of Covid-19. Some, like Sol Campbell, have suggested that the pandemic was in some way man-made. Icke is in the camp which believes that the lockdown and vaccination scheme was akin to governmental 'facism'. Lovren was firmly in team Icke during the lockdown years, posting a number of his videos on social media. He also used social media to attack Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates, implying some kind of conspiracy with his comment: 'Game over Bill. People are not blind' on Gates's online tribute to health workers. The Croatian defender seemed particularly swayed by Icke's theories around the links between Covid-19 and 5G technology in 'controlling' populations, with Lovren resharing clips with the caption 'we will not be censored'. Dejan Lovren supported Icke's views during the pandemic and hit out at Bill Gates Lovren took to Instagram to promote an interview with Icke during the pandemic CB: Sol Campbell As mentioned in Lovren's section, Campbell also had his suspicions during the Covid-19 pandemic. Then managing Southend United, in May 2020, Campbell appeared to suggest that he believed the disease was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups. 'Was this virus a natural mistake or a designed mistake...?' he posted on social media. 'I wonder does this virus deliberately attacks a certain blood type.....?' Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group. He later was widely derided for having no scientific evidence to support his argument. Sol Campbell appeared to suggest in 2020 he believed Covid-`9 was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group LB: Fabian Delph The former Manchester City defender has previously admitted to a conspiracy theory that has more sympathetic readers nodding in approval: he believes in ghosts. Delph admitted in 2016 that he sees ghosts 'all the time', adding that 'genuinely' he had seen about 'four'. 'When I first signed for (Aston) Villa I stayed in a hotel there was lots of things moving in the room, a lot of bangs,' he told Man City's official YouTube channel. 'And about four months ago I saw, in my house in God's country (Yorkshire), I saw two ghosts in my bedroom.' 'I don't think they're there to harm me. But I've definitely seen them. It was just a split second and then they were gone. 'The one four months ago, that actually was carrying a body, it went out onto my balcony, then disappeared.' Joe Cole admitted he is open to having his head turnedabout the moon landings and would be keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong to 'get to the bottom of things' RM: Joe Cole Compared to how some of the other members of Daily Mail Sport's XI have at times risked public safety or aired unpleasant and divisive views, Cole's position on the 1969 Moon Landings feels somewhat milquetoast. Additionally, unlike many, he admitted that he is open to having his head turned, with Cole keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong, the first man on the moon, to 'get to the bottom' of things. 'I'm not sold either way and I need some convincing. I want to believe it, honestly,' Cole told FourFourTwo. 'But I've heard too much about it being fake - things like the flag waving and the footprints and all the rest of it. 'I would love to sit down with a man who actually went there and be convinced. I want him to tell me exactly how it all went down and some of the science behind my questions. 'I just want to put it to bed. If anyone could convince me, it's the first man to have apparently visited the moon. I don't mind being talked round to new ideas which is why I'd be more than happy for him to tell me how silly I'm being. 'That's what makes you evolve as a human being. You have to be open to different ideas in life.' CM: Marcos Llorente If Pove represents a distinctly Spanish-style conspiracy theorist, Marcos Llorente treads the well-beaten path, with his primary focus the benefits of sunlight – to the extent of snubbing suncream – and a suspicion of 'chemtrails'. Llorente takes his theories on natural light and the sun to the extreme, however. A staunch advocate of the blue light-blocking sunglasses also favoured by stars including Erling Haaland, the Atletico Madrid midfielder also eschews unnatural light sources in his house after dark. Instead, Llorente works on soaking up as much red light as possible. In the sun, Llorente takes it one step further, frequently sharing incorrect views on suncream's impact on Vitamin D and dismissing the connection between skin cancer and unprotected skin. Marcos Llorente is a committed wearer of blue light-blocking glasses in a bid to boost his melatonin Llorente has frequently endorsed the repeatedly debunked theory that 'chemtrails' are the result of government or corporate intervention Llorente often does so in a tongue-in-cheek way: in April, he dressed up as a bottle of suncream, but with a twist. Written on the bottle in Spanish were messages reading: 'Protect against your biology' and 'Blocking Vitamin D since 1985'. On the back of the bottle costume in lieu of ingredients, Llorente drew a graph of rising skin cancer rates and an accompanying message. 'Get in the shade when your body tells you, 'That's enough'. Get sun exposure year-round, not just three days in August,' the 'warning label' read. 'Use clothing as sun protection. Start in the morning and work your way up (don't start at 1pm). 'Build melanin gradually. Eat a balanced diet so your skin responds better. Stay hydrated and connect with nature.' More recently Llorente, a bon viveur and lover of rare steak, 'bulletproof' butter coffee and good wine, has intensified his stance on other medical theories, including alleging that high cholesterol or 'bad' cholesterol does not have an impact on health. CM: Matt Le Tissier Matt Le Tissier is no single-issue conspiracy theorist, with the Southampton icon borderline indiscriminate about the wide range of his causes. Like many, his outpourings amplified amid the pandemic, with Le Tissier frequently opining on the efficacy of vaccines and painting 'big pharma' as a bogeyman. Then, in 2022, he was stood down from his role as Saints ambassador after peddling Russian lies that the massacre at Bucha, in Ukraine, had been fabricated. This came despite the fact that there was video, satellite, and photographic evidence that Russia had murdered over 320 people in the town. Earlier this year, Le Tissier found himself in a spat with Grok, X's AI chatbot, over 'chemtrails', asking: 'Hey (Grok), why do some plane trails disperse quickly while others hang around and spread out to form grey blanket clouds?' The bot had responded that the contrails lingered or didn't due to atmospheric conditions, much to Le Tissier's displeasure, with the former midfielder grumbling that Grok was 'spouting government propaganda'. Matt Le Tissier, pictured taking a selfie at a Southampton game in February, has frequently raised conspiracy theories over social media

Your browser does not support iframes.

LM: David Cotterill Former Wales international David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas. Cotterill said in the incendiary post that 'false flag events are one of their go to methods of manipulating the public opinion to bring about change'. He also alleged: 'America is the last major country that allows it's [sic] citizens to arm themselves. Which they can't really have with what they're planning to do in the coming months and years.' Cotterill later stressed that the post had not been related to the Texas massacre, instead stating that his post was 'just about recent articles when you see some of the stuff about the pandemic'. He similarly received intense criticism when he suggested that the retirement of Brighton's 24-year-old Enock Mwepu due to cardiac issues was linked to side effect of the Covid-19 vaccine. Cotterill remains unrepentant however, recently appearing on a podcast where he admitted that he supports 'everything' Le Tissier says, and revealed his belief in 2016's discredited Pizzagate conspiracy, among other conspiracy theories. 'I've gone into so many rabbit holes. If you see lots of things happening in the world with the number 33, which is obviously massive for Freemasonry and symbolism,' he told Made in Brum Podcast. 'If you see a lot of things that happen in the world, 33 is not far from that. Some people think I'm f***ing nuts. David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas ST: Rickie Lambert Former Liverpool and Southampton star Rickie Lambert is among this cohort's Covid-19 conspiracy theorists, starting off on social media as a staunch vaccine sceptic - only to fall deeper into more fringe views. Unusually, in 2023, Lambert claimed that he believed that one can change the molecular structure of water based on speaking to a glass of the substance positively or negatively. 'The one word where water responds in the most beautiful way, with the most beautiful crystals, is showing gratitude to water,' Lambert said. More recently, Lambert has been an active supporter of the campaign against '15-minute cities', whose detractors believe is a government scheme to control the movement and rights of people, rather than an attempt to provide walkable goods and services. Ahead of attending a protest in Liverpool in September 2023, Lambert's call to arms to publicise the event stressed that the scheme was 'a controlled tactic being implemented across this country' and that Merseyside was set to be put under permanent surveillance. Rickie Lambert has claimed talking positively to water makes it clean ST: Robbie Fowler Like Cole, Fowler appears to have merely dipped a toe into the world of conspiratorial thinking, and has similarly alighted on the Moon Landing as the target of his suspicion. Unlike the former Chelsea star however, there seemed to be little that would change his mind when he discussed the topic with his We'll Have A Look podcast with co-host Steve McManaman. 'I think the Moon Landing is bulls***, to be fair,' Fowler said. 'Because there was a race in the Sixties, between the Americans and the USSR. 'All of a sudden, the USSR were ahead of the Americans (after Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space) and all of a sudden, the Americans got there first. 'I think it's a bit far-fetched. I don't know, that is the general gist of what I'm saying - I just don't think it was real.'

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola has Liverpool's fearsome frontline firing, Alexis Mac Allister back to his best and is unlocking the best of Florian Wirtz... it is far too soon to count them out of the title race, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has Liverpool's fearsome frontline firing, Alexis Mac Allister back to his best and is unlocking the best of Florian Wirtz... it is far too soon to count them out of the title race, writes LEWIS STEELE

Are Liverpool in the title race? The question has been bandied around this week — and conversations will only grow louder if they beat Arsenal at Anfield tomorrow.

The clash feels like an early six-pointer but regardless of the result, we can make this point — Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are on the up and, whether this year or next, will soon be competing for the top prizes again.

This follows a season of strife in which the football was boring, the title defence fell apart and fans turned mutinous — booing, leaving early and moaning at manager Arne Slot.

The Dutchman paid with his job and in came Iraola, who — with respect to Bournemouth and Rayo Vallecano — had no experience of managing the day-to-day stresses and demands of a club of this size.

Three months into his reign, the Basque is yet to receive the plaudits he deserves. Maybe because Arsenal are champions and the two Manchester clubs are never out of the headlines, Liverpool have gone under the radar.

But they have lost just once, when down to 10 men against Manchester City, and have won their last five games, including some potential banana skins. So is it time to stop sleeping on this team’s chances?

Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are on the up and will soon be competing for the top prizes again

Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola are starting to fire for Iraola

We can go position by position and analyse how the Reds have improved under Iraola. In attack, there was a potential narrative of a post-Mohamed Salah slump, but the absence of the Egyptian has rarely been mentioned.

In the summer, Iraola said he wants his forwards to be ‘game changers’ and he has plenty of those — Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Rio Ngumoha have all fulfilled that role, plus Hugo Ekitike when he returns from injury.

In midfield, Alexis Mac Allister is back to his best and Iraola sees the Argentine as his coach on the pitch, a man who reads the game better than anyone. Wirtz is getting better while young Trey Nyoni, 19, has been outstanding when he has featured.

At the back, Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation. Fellow new signing Ronald Araujo is only on loan from Barcelona — there is an option to make that permanent — but is becoming a cult hero.

Iraola has also got the fans back on side. It is fair to say the Kop was unsure of him when he arrived but he has won them over with a front-footed, exciting style in a system that demands hard work and relentless pressing.

There is the perfect blend of youth and experience and it is clear the team are fighting for one another again.

‘It’s not just winning,’ Iraola said. ‘At Anfield, everyone feels when the team goes for it and when everyone is giving everything, trying his best… then the supporters will be there. Even when we have been losing, they have helped us massively.’

Florian Wirtz endured a difficult first season at Anfield but is starting to show why the club paid big money to sign him from Bayer Leverkusen in 2025

Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation in the Liverpool defence

Captain Virgil van Dijk added: ‘The fans definitely like what they’re seeing and, of course, you feel that energy and it’s great. I’ve been feeling that energy for quite a while and when you miss it then to get it back is obviously very good.’

So, title race? Absolutely. Beat Arsenal and they are only three points behind the Gunners, so why not? Lose and it is nine points, which would not be insurmountable with 29 games and six months to go, but would certainly reduce the margin for error.

Usurping the Gunners might be a step too far this season, but Liverpool are certainly stronger than last term — and Iraola says there is still plenty of room for improvement.

Just look at his Bournemouth side. Winless in their first nine games, they barely looked back as they qualified for Europe. Liverpool had a rocky first month with obvious deficiencies, but are now building a head of steam.

Arsenal visit on Sunday having not won at Anfield since 2012 - last season this fixture was won by Dominik Szoboszlai's stunning 35-yard free-kick

The small details are also improving, such as solidity from set-pieces — an issue that bugged them last term with a league-high 20 goals conceded. The fitness of Isak is a huge factor, while Alisson looks in top condition again.

Asked where his team can improve, Iraola said: ‘Almost everywhere. We are defending really well lately but still we have some situations where we need to improve. In the league, we have been less dangerous offensively.

‘So it is still too early to make big conclusions but there are improvements needed everywhere.’

Arsenal might not be wary of Manchester City given potential points deductions but, should Liverpool beat them on Halloween weekend, the champions will certainly be running scared.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies.
