More than 100 officers were injured, one of them seriously, during violent confrontations in Frankfurt after largely peaceful demonstrations on Saturday, according to Roman Poseck, the interior minister in the state of Hesse, where Frankfurt is located.

He added that up to 1,300 officers were on duty in Frankfurt on Saturday night and into Sunday morning.

The minister said 17 stores were damaged and five were looted. Police took 54 people into custody, all between the ages of 13 and 29.

Of the more than 8,000 people who took part in the protests in Frankfurt, authorities estimated there were 1,000 to 1,500 violent troublemakers, "predominantly from a migrant background."

Poseck said, "An enormous potential for violence on the part of left-wing extremists and violence-prone young people, mostly from migrant backgrounds, has been unleashed."

"This group of offenders was predominantly made up of migrants. And we must address that too," he added. "There must be no false taboos here."

After blaming migrants for the violence, Poseck said German citizens made up the vast majority of those detained.

In Cologne, which also saw violent confrontations between rioters and police, state Interior Minister Herbert Reul said left-wing extremists hijacked the Gen Z protests.

"Anyone who throws rocks and firecrackers at police officers, sets off fireworks, and rampages through the streets has no political agenda," Reul said in a statement. "People who cover their faces don't want to discuss or persuade. They want trouble and violence. There’s no justification for that."

World.title: Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease
World.content:
Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. But new developments in biotech and AI are a cause for concern. DW addresses some of the most important questions about their history, risks, and control.

Artificial intelligence could potentially be misused to develop biological weapons. This may sound like science fiction, but scientists, security services, and international organizations are all looking at how to deal with this scenario.

Pathogens can be analyzed and altered with ever greater precision thanks to ongoing developments in biotechnology. Meanwhile, AI is able to evaluate vast quantities of data at astonishing speeds. As a result, experts are warning that, in the long term, modern technologies could also be misused to develop biological weapons.

Security services are concerned. In October 2026, Ken McCallum, head of the British domestic intelligence service MI5, warned that artificial intelligence could increase the risk from existing, or new, biological weapons – including from non-state actors.

Fine line between valid research and misuse

A report by the American AI company Anthropic in September 2026 highlights the topicality of the debate. Anthropic said it had identified and blocked numerous attempts to use its AI assistant Claude in connection with possible biological weapon research. The report said these attempts included grant applications for so-called "gain-of-function" research, as well as projects to research avian influenza variants that were potentially the most transmissible to mammals.

At the same time, Anthropic stressed that, although it could have a military application, such research could also relate to medical prevention. The difficulty in distinguishing between legitimate science and its possible misuse is one of the biggest problems in terms of the control of modern biotechnologies.

What are biological weapons?

Concerns about biological weapons are by no means new. Many pathogens — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and certain biological toxins — have the potential for weaponization. Familiar diseases include plague, smallpox, and botulinum toxin, but anthrax is one of the most notorious biological agents. Its resistant spores can survive a long time in the environment, and it has also been the focus of research by state biological weapons programs.

Melting ice brings new dangers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs define a biological weapon as the targeted release of such biological substances for the purpose of injuring people, animals, or plants.

A biological weapon usually has two components: The biological substance itself, and a system for disseminating it. Experts refer to these as the "agent," such as a virus or bacterium, and the "delivery mechanism." Examples of the latter include missiles, spraying systems, and contaminated food.

Biological weapons belong to the so-called ABC weapons, alongside atomic (nuclear) and chemical weapons. They are often also counted as weapons of mass destruction.

How do they differ from chemical weapons?

Biological and chemical weapons differ in their mode of operation. Chemical weapons injure people through the toxic effects of chemical substances such as sarin or mustard gas. They will often take effect within minutes, or even seconds. Examples of the use of chemical weapons are the gas attacks in World War I, which involved chlorine gas, and later mustard gas; and the deployment of the nerve gas sarin in the Syrian civil war and by Saddam Hussein in Iraq.

Biological weapons, on the other hand, cause infectious disease. The effects become apparent only hours, days, or even weeks after they have been deployed. Some pathogens are also capable of spreading from person to person, meaning that the outcome is difficult to predict.

To summarize: Chemical weapons kill or injure through immediate toxicity, whereas biological weapons cause diseases. The possibility of human-to-human transmission makes the effect of a biological weapon particularly hard to calculate.

Are biological weapons subject to a worldwide ban?

Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. The first Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) came into force in 1975. This prohibits the development, stockpiling, acquisition, retention, production, and transfer of biological and toxin-based weapons.

The Convention, which has been ratified by 189 countries, can be seen as a development of the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which banned the use of biological weapons as a method of warfare. Only a few countries have not signed the agreement , or have signed but not ratified it, including Israel, Egypt, and Syria. All those who have acceded to the Convention have also committed themselves to destroying all stocks, production sites, and means of conveyance.

Chemical weapons are also internationally banned, but their control is seen as much more highly developed. The Chemical Weapons Convention is implemented by the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW ), which can carry out inspections and oversee the destruction of chemical weapons stocks.

There is still no comparable system for controlling biological weapons. States fear that inspection could expose sensitive research data pertaining to medicine, biotechnology, or the pharmaceutical industry. This is why the control of biological weapons relies to a great extent on transparency, voluntary reporting, and good faith.

One of the best-known examples of why the ban on biological weapons is insufficient on its own to prevent their use occurred in the United States in 2001. A few weeks after the attacks of September 11, several people received letters containing anthrax spores. 22 were infected, and five died.

Million-dollar reward: In 2001, anthrax was sent by post to several prominent Americans in an act of domestic terrorism Image: USPS/dpa/picture alliance

Why are biological weapons so hard to expose and control?

Finding biological weapons programs is much harder than controlling the production of nuclear or chemical weapons. Many technologies that could be used to develop biological weapons also have civilian applications. The same laboratory equipment used to develop vaccines and medicines could, in theory, also be used for military research.

Experts refer to this as the problem of dual use. Research can be done for peaceful medical purposes and, at the same time, have a military application.

Furthermore, a biological attack can initially look like a natural outbreak of disease. It is often only possible after extensive investigation to establish whether a pathogen was deliberately released or occurred naturally.

Perhaps that is also why biological weapons have been deployed at various times throughout history. Historical reports range from the poisoning of wells to catapulting the corpses of plague victims over the walls of a besieged town. The effectiveness of these methods is, however, disputed.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Portugal police storm housing protest camps in Lisbon, Porto
World.content:
Clashes broke out as officers again dispersed housing protesters from tent camps in Lisbon and Porto. Portuguese police have repeatedly cleared tent camps erected across both cities in recent weeks.

Police on Sunday cleared out protest camps in Portugal's capital, Lisbon, and Porto after thousands of housing protesters marched against a rental bill.

Around 4:30 a.m. local time (0430 GMT), ‌dozens of officers moved in to dismantle camps in Lisbon's Rossio Square and Porto's Dom Joao I Square, where participants had set up tents following peaceful marches against soaring housing costs on Saturday.

Police used shields and batons to disperse protesters, and said some of the demonstrators threw bottles and paint at officers as they stormed the camps.

Dozens were reportedly injured after riot police clashed with housing protesters Image: Filipe Amorim/AFP

Police arrest 13 in Lisbon, Porto

Six people were arrested in Lisbon and seven in Porto for refusing orders to disperse, according to a police statement. It said 13 police were injured as they tried to take down the camps, with eight taken to hospital.

The statement also said an unspecified number of civilians were also injured.

Meanwhile, one of the lawyers representing those detained in Porto said the police response was disproportionate, arguing that both the size of the operation and the actions were excessive.

Activist group Acampada Lisboa said more than 30 protesters were injured, including 10 who required hospital treatment.

It called a fresh rally against the police operation in the capital on Sunday afternoon. "We will not be silenced," the group said in a statement posted on social media.

Portugal's housing crisis

Hours before the eviction, more than 1,000 people marched through central Lisbon to protest against Portugal's deepening housing crisis.

Demonstrators are calling for the country's minority center-right government to scrap plans that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases.

Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has ruled out withdrawing the bill, though he has acknowledged that modifications could be made before the final vote.

Portugal is facing one of Europe's most severe housing crises, with house prices more than doubling since 2017.

World.title: India news: Opposition holds major rally in Delhi over voter roll revisions

Thousands gathered to protest a controversial revision of India's electoral rolls Image: Ab Rauoof Ganie/DW

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would be removed from office and jailed, accusing him of facilitating electoral fraud.

Speaking at a rally organized by the opposition INDIA alliance in New Delhi, Gandhi alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah owed their positions to Kumar.

"Gyanesh Kumar will be removed from the post of Chief Election Commissioner. Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail," Gandhi told supporters.

The Congress leader also accused authorities of manipulating elections through electronic voting machines and changes to electoral rolls.

"For years, vote theft has been happening in this country," Gandhi said, citing several state elections and the 2024 parliamentary vote.

He further claimed that 15% of India's voters had been removed from electoral rolls following the 2024 election. The allegations have not been independently verified.

Gandhi also criticized economic inequality and the treatment of farmers, young people and workers.

"The farmer is not getting his rights. The youth are not getting employment. The laborer is not getting his rights, and the entire wealth has gone into the hands of two or three people," he said.

World.title: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
World.content:
Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.

The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.

But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva, in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.

In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic. And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.

Trump ally and former president Aleksandar Vucic was defeated in Serbia's parliamentary election on October 25 Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."

Trump declared Brazilian election looked "rigged"

Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida. The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.

Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."

How secure are the US midterm elections? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Good relations with Putin ally Vucic

Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.

The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.

Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.

Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a "humanitarian," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.

Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israel: Outcome still unclear

There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.

Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.

Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power, little, if anything, will change.

Israeli's right-wing leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, highlighted his closeness to Trump in his election campaign Image: Oded Balilty/AP Photo/picture alliance

No rosy prospects for Trump in the midterms

With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."

But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."

Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.

World.title: Tras las huellas de Miguel Hernández, con el Guadalquivir y el Segura como compañeros de viaje
World.content:
La casa museo de Miguel Hernández en Orihuela, donde vivió con su familia entre 1914 y 1934.

Ruta por las dos patrias del poeta, Alicante y Jaén, por el 116º aniversario de su nacimiento

Este viernes 30 de octubre se cumplen 116 años del nacimiento de Miguel Hernández, un poeta universal al que dejaron morir en la cárcel de Alicante al acabar la Guerra Civil cuando apenas tenía 31 años. La obra hernandiana tiene dos referentes geográficos: su cuna e infancia oriolanas y alicantinas, de un lado, y, de otro, la provincia de Jaén, adonde llegó destinado como comisario de Cultura para dirigir el periódico Altavoz del Frente Sur. De allí era su esposa, Josefina Manresa, y aquí fue nombrado en 2024 Hijo Adoptivo de la provincia a título póstumo.

Estas dos patrias del poeta son el argumento de una ruta turística que tiene a los ríos Guadalquivir y Segura como compañeros de viaje. El Guadalquivir por nacer en el municipio de Quesada, donde se encuentra el Museo Miguel Hernández-Josefina Manresa, y el Segura por ser el río que, desde su nacimiento en Pontones, en la jiennense sierra de Segura, mejor vertebra a los dos territorios hernandianos por excelencia.

Más información De Sitges a Montserrat: cuatro escapadas en los alrededores de Barcelona

La Senda del Poeta, o camino hernandiano, es una ruta que conecta los lugares que marcaron la vida y la obra de Miguel Hernández (1910-1942), un itinerario que arranca en Jaén, donde se encuentra actualmente el legado que conservó su mujer, y que sigue el curso del río Segura hasta llegar a su desembocadura, en Guardamar del Segura (Alicante). A través del sendero GR-125 el itinerario atraviesa varios pueblos levantinos por donde transcurrió la infancia y también los últimos años de vida de Miguel Hernández.

Iniciamos el viaje en Jaén, donde la Diputación adquirió en 2012 el legado personal del poeta, que está compuesto por 5.819 registros bibliográficos y 26.684 imágenes, entre los que se encuentran documentos personales, manuscritos y correspondencia, borradores de sus obras; recortes de prensa, libros, grabaciones sonoras; dibujos, grabados y carteles; y objetos representativos como su máquina de escribir, la maleta o la lechera en la que le pasaba a su esposa Josefina cartas y poemas desde la cárcel. Este legado está repartido entre el Instituto de Estudios Giennenses y el Museo Miguel Hernández-Josefina Manresa de Quesada.

El Instituto de Estudios Giennenses (IEG) es una de las tres patas de un triángulo monumental que forman el Antiguo Hospital de San Juan de Dios (donde se encuentra su sede), los Baños Árabes del Palacio de Villardompardo y la iglesia de Santa Catalina Mártir, junto al antiguo convento de Santo Domingo.

Santo Domingo es el resultado de un proceso constructivo prolongado entre finales del siglo XV y el último tercio del siglo XVI. Sobre algunos de los palacios islámicos previos se comenzó a levantar una iglesia tardogótica de la que aún perviven elementos como la capilla mayor y algunas bóvedas. Entre 1575 y 1582 continuaron las obras del templo y se siguió un nuevo proyecto manierista, configurando la nave, el coro y la portada actual.

Claustro del monasterio de Santo Domingo, en Jaén. diego grandi ( GETTY IMAGES )

La conexión del poeta alicantino con Jaén se inició cuando fue destinado como comisario de Cultura para dirigir el periódico Altavoz del Frente Sur. Coincidiendo con el 84º aniversario de su muerte, la ciudad de Jaén estrenó una ruta literaria que recorre los lugares de su estancia en tierras jiennenses, desde la plaza de los Naranjos, bautizada también como plaza de Miguel Hernández, y que continúa por el refugio antiaéreo de la plaza de Santiago, donde se rememora el bombardeo de Jaén del 1 de abril de 1937 que se saldó con 159 muertos y decenas de heridos. Cuando el bombardeo de Jaén, Miguel Hernández se encontraba fuera cubriendo la batalla de Peñarroya o en la defensa de Medellín, pero Josefina Manresa sí que fue testigo directo.

El otro pilar clave fue su esposa, que era natural de Quesada, localidad que es la cuna del río Guadalquivir y donde desde el año 2015 hay un museo en memoria de los dos. Tras convertirse en la viuda de un poeta maldito, Josefina guardó celosamente los escritos de Miguel, como centinela de su memoria, para que nadie pudiera arrebatarle ese tesoro; documentos de su marido que durante años mantuvo escondidos en costales de los que se utilizaban para llenar el trigo. En el museo quesadeño, que comparte instalaciones con el dedicado al pintor Rafael Zabaleta, se hace un recorrido por la obra y la vida del poeta y su esposa, una historia de amor llena de pasiones y emociones. Como esta carta en la que ella relata sus primeros encuentros: “Me estuvo pretendiendo desde el año 1933 hasta el 27 de septiembre del 34. Pasaba varias veces por la puerta del taller de la calle Mayor, en Orihuela, donde yo trabajaba de modista. Miraba hacia dentro del taller y me di cuenta que me miraba a mí”.

Su estancia en Jaén fue la que inspiró otro de sus poemas más célebres, Aceituneros, que pone letra al himno de la provincia. La coral Encina Hermosa, de Castillo de Locubín, lo ha versionado ahora en clave feminista:

Andaluzas de Jaén

aceituneras comprometidas

decidme en el alma: ¿quién

recogió las olivas?

No las recogió la nada,

ni el dinero, ni el señor

sino la mujer arrastrada,

el cariño y el tesón

Conectada a la luna

y a la rociá de la mañana

las tres dieron la vida

a ese olivo y a sus ramas

Levántate aceitunera de plata

decimos al pie del viento

la aceitunera alzó su mano

poderosa de miramiento

Andaluzas de Jaén

aceituneras comprometidas

decidme en el alma: ¿quién

amamantó los olivos?

Nuestra sangre, nuestro cuerpo

no sólo la del hombre

que se llevó el mérito

de nuestro sufrimiento

Andaluzas, levantémonos

reclamemos nuestro lugar

La fachada de la fundación Miguel Hernández, en Orihuela, donde nació el poeta. mauritius images/ Alamy / CORDON PRESS

Siguiendo la Senda del Poeta

Ya en la provincia de Alicante, y con el río Segura como compañero de viaje, nos adentramos en la llamada Senda del Poeta creada por varias instituciones levantinas en homenaje al escritor, natural de Orihuela. Este itinerario, que puede realizarse en cualquier época del año, se efectúa a pie durante tres días desde la Casa Museo de Miguel Hernández en Orihuela hasta su tumba en el cementerio de Alicante.

Esta ruta, que atraviesa el sendero de gran recorrido GR-125, está dividida en tres etapas. Arranca en Orihuela, ciudad donde nació Miguel Hernández el 30 de octubre de 1910. Orihuela marcó su infancia y juventud de forma decisiva, ya que aquí fue donde inició sus estudios escolares en el colegio Santo Domingo, ayudó a su padre en los trabajos de pastoreo, participó en las reuniones literarias de la tahona de los hermanos Fenoll, publicó sus primeros poemas y conoció a Josefina Manresa. A continuación, se pasa por Redován, donde nació su progenitor, por Callosa del Segura, se llega a Cox, donde Hernández y Manresa vivieron varios años; por Elche, donde murieron su mujer e hijo, y concluye en Alicante.

La primera etapa transcurre también por Granja de Rocamora y finaliza en Albatera, en cuyo término se encontraba el campo de concentración donde perecieron muchos compañeros de Hernández tras la Guerra Civil. Todo ello por caminos con numerosos huertos de naranjos y limoneros que ofrecen al caminante el penetrante olor del azahar, característico de la primavera en la vega baja del río Segura.

La segunda etapa del sendero, entre caminos donde predominan las palmeras, transcurre entre Albatera y Elche, adonde se trasladó Josefina Manresa con su hijo Manuel Miguel tras la muerte del poeta. En el Archivo Municipal de Elche se encuentran depositados un buen número de manuscritos del poeta y aquí también se encuentra la Universidad pública Miguel Hernández que, en 1998, nombró al poeta Doctor Honoris Causa a título póstumo.

El palmeral de la ciudad de Elche, una de las paradas siguiendo las huellas de Miguel Hernández. José Antonio Aldeguer ( GETTY IMAGES )

Finalmente, la tercera y última etapa discurre entre Elche y Alicante, en cuya cárcel falleció el 28 de marzo de 1942. Aquí redactó sus últimos poemas de Cancionero y romancero de ausencias, y en las dependencias de la enfermería carcelaria contrajo matrimonio canónico con Josefina Manresa días antes de morir.

En el cementerio de Alicante, entre campos de almendros, reposan los restos del poeta en una tumba en donde también se encuentran enterrados su mujer y su hijo.

World.title: From pickles to magic: 11 great things to do in November
World.content:
It’s November, the quiet before the Christmas cheer storm. But there’s still much non-festive fun to be had, as the list will show.

Make a night of it

It’s Museumnacht in Amsterdam this month. Some 65 museums are keeping their doors open and there is a raft of night-time activities, including Ask an Imam where visitors can discuss matters of faith, a trip on a boat used by refugees, and many more. November 7. Website

Spot the differences

The Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem is planning its own blockbuster exhibition with the succinctly named Hals-Rembrandt, which focuses on the differences and similarities in the styles of the two Dutch 17th-century masters. The museum will open earlier and use time slots to give visitors the opportunity for a proper gaze at the juxtaposed works. From November 6. Website

See ancient Egypt come to life

The Olympisch Stadion in Amsterdam is hosting Tutankhamun – the immersive exhibition, where VR wizardry takes you to the heart of ancient Egypt without getting sand between your toes. It’s a pretty amazing spectacle and children will love it too. From November 6. Website

Spare five minutes

The Orange Theatre Company presents a series of five-minute English language monologues around the theme ‘In the Flesh’ as part of its Tiny Theatre programme. It’s all about desire, so it might get a bit steamy in the Oedipus Brewery in Amsterdam. November 11. Website

Get into a pickle

It’s American Pickle Day on November 14 and Amsterdam, like New York, a traditional pickle city, is getting in on the act. A Big Dill celebrates that history with an exhibition of pickle paintings by New York painter Harvey Herman, himself a member of the Tannenbaum pickle family and a former seller of “pickles for a nickel”, pickle history from both cities and, of course, pickle tastings. It’s on at the st-Art Centre in Amsterdam-West. November 14. Website

Praat Nederlands

People from the Leiden region are invited to join fellow expats/immigrants/internationals struggling to learn the language and speak Dutch all day long. Practise Dutch in “a safe space” to boost your confidence and meet like-minded folk to have a good moan about the pitfalls of this wonderful and useful language. There are activities as well. November 26. Website

Catch Shrek in Amsterdam

Grab your chance to take the nippers to Shrek The Musical, the jolly story of the ogre, the princess and the talking donkey. It’s on at the Amsterdams Theaterhuis and we are including the December dates in case you want to avoid the December festive reservation surge. It’s in English, by the way. November 27-29, December 3-6. Website

Say hi to the Sint at Soestdijk

Sinterklaas is always met with a warm welcome in the Netherlands and that includes a well-deserved stay at the sumptuous, former royal palace Paleis Soestdijk. The Sint will not just be luxuriating in a royal bathtub, of course. The Blue Corridor (the former royal residence) has been turned into a Pieten Palace where Pieten are busy sorting out the presents and poems for December 5. Sinterklaas will make time for children wanting to see him, and they can even take a peek at his bedroom and do lots of activities. Children can bring a drawing to butter the Sint up. November 27, 28, 29. Website

See the seedy side of the Herengracht

The opulence of the houses on Amsterdam’s Herengracht finds its origin in the slave trade. Number 605, now the Willet-Holthuysen museum, named after its last owners who left the double canal house and its contents to the city, is a good example. Previous owners financier Willem Deutz (1697-1757) and merchant Fredrik Berewout (1692-1777) grew massively rich on the profits made from the slave trade, as the current exhibition Plantation along the Canal makes clear. Among the exhibits is a complete inventory of the Jagtlust plantation in Suriname, owned by Berewout, including the names and value of 125 slaves. Until April 4. Website

Find out how it’s done

Abracadabra, at the Jewish Museum in Amsterdam, is a fascinating look at the world of Jewish illusionists around 1900. The “Golden Age of Magic” included such famous names as escape artist Harry Houdini, and Horace Goldin and Okito (the stage name of Dutch magician Theo Bamberg) among others. World-renowned Dutch illusionist and collector Hans Klok became the chosen recipient of Bamberg’s tricks of the trade and decided to share them with the world, along with other magicians’ lore. Klok himself puts in an appearance on video to explain some of the tricks and visitors are invited to have a go as well. Until March 29, 2027. Website

Mind your ankles

Yay! Get your platform shoes on and dance to the music of the 70s at the Wereldmuseum in Amsterdam. There is much more to disco than glitter and glam. Its history is tied up with the emancipation of gays, queers, Latinos and other marginalised groups who created their own fabulous world of music and art. You can bop your way through hundreds of disco tracks, videos, artworks, fashion pieces and design objects, including works by Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, Kwame Brathwaite, Michael Abramson, Meryl Meisler and many others. Until August 22, 2027. Website

World.title: Fears spread over Gen Z riot plans across NL
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

There are fears that a “Gen Z” protest, inspired by the ongoing unrest that has swept through France and other countries, could hit the Netherlands over the weekend.

A report in AD found that groups on Telegram, Snapchat and other social media platforms are preparing to riot in cities including The Hague, Maastricht and Eindhoven.

While no applications for protest permits have been submitted, police have said they generally monitor online forums for signs of trouble but would not comment on this matter specifically.

The messages, which include calls to loot shopping centres, were enough to prompt school heads to issue warnings to parents in Maastricht. Limburg police backed the warnings, according to local broadcaster L1 News.

Shopkeepers in The Hague have also started boarding up their windows as a precaution, as some messaging groups are calling for gatherings on the Malieveld and attacks on commercial centres nearby, according to Omroep West.

The protests in France, which have spread to Italy and Spain began over education and living standards among young people. Many of the demonstrations quickly descended into serious rioting, often with heavy police response.

There are similar concerns in Germany, where youth groups are preparing to protest over similar issues on Halloween.

World.title: “No movement” in cabinet talks amid left-right stalemate
World.content:
The cabinet’s attempt to win over left- and right-wing opposition parties in its ongoing tax plan talks failed again on Friday.

Prime minister Rob Jetten and other senior ministers met opposition leaders a day after three right-wing parties, the far-right JA21, orthodox Protestant SGP and farmer-citizen movement BBB, banded together to push their demands as a single bloc. The demands range from harsher asylum measures and changes to abortion rules to scrapping a tax rise to pay for defence.

The move was the latest attempt by the opposition to force the cabinet to pick a side. Opposition parties have said for weeks that the cabinet will never get a broad agreement, because the two sides of the aisle have incompatible demands.

The offer presented on Friday covered how to pay for changes to box 3, the tax on savings and investments, without raising taxes on wealth, sources told the Telegraaf.

The cabinet would use money left over from a fund to refund people who were overtaxed under box 3 in past years, and cut taxes for business owners who pay themselves profits from their own companies. It would also keep a tax deduction for healthcare costs that was due to be scrapped in 2028.

Regardless of the offer, the stalemate appears to continue. Centre-left PRO leader Jesse Klaver said he saw “no movement at all” on his party’s demand for higher taxes on the wealthy and lower taxes on workers.

JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans called it “a tough, complicated conversation”, but said the new right-wing alliance remained intact.

The coalition of D66, VVD and CDA does not have a majority, so it needs support from opposition parties to get its tax plan through parliament.

World.title: Government seeks to ban smoking where children congregate
World.content:
The Dutch cabinet wants to prohibit smoking at locations dominated by children, including petting zoos and after-school and other managed playgrounds.

Sources told broadcaster NOS the proposed ban will be discussed at Friday’s Council of Ministers.

While most such places are already smoke-free, the government wants to ensure that the remaining few ban smoking. The House of Representatives also supports the ban and wanted to extend it to other kid-friendly locations like zoos and amusement parks.

That may come in the future, along with bans at unattended playgrounds and outdoor swimming pools, but for now, the government will focus on managed playgrounds and day care centres where there is wide support for the plan.

The ban is part of the government’s efforts to have a smoke-free generation by 2040. Measures already in place include a display ban, unattractive packaging and fewer locations to purchase cigarettes.

World.title: Herman Brood painting added to national art collection
World.content:
A painting by rock legend and artist Herman Brood has been added to the National Collection, placing Brood in the company of Dutch icons such as Rembrandt, Ferdinand Bol, Piet Mondriaan and Karel Appel.

“We believe that Herman Brood should be given more prestige as an icon of the twentieth century as an artist,” said the cultural heritage anency (RCE).

The untitled acrylic work, made with an ever-present injection syringe and paint rollers, features two men with a pistol. It has been hanging on the wall of the tax office in The Hague but was moved earlier this week to the RCE’s depot in Amersfoort, where it’s been given the name “rock-‘n-roll on canvas”.

The inclusion of the work in the 120,000-strong national collection is official recognition that Brood has contributed substantially to Dutch culture and history. The work will be preserved permenantly and can be lent to museums.

“Junkie who painted”

Rob Dupré, a friend of “The Never Be Clever” and “Saturday Night” singer who died in 2001, told broadcaster NOS that Brood would rise from the dead if he heard the news.

“In life, he was seen as a rock ‘n’ roll singer who worked as an artist. Others called him a junkie who painted. As if everyone could do what he did. This news is like winning gold at the Olympics,” said Dupré, who works to detect counterfeits attributed to the artist.

It’s thought the painting ended up in the tax office to pay off a debt. “He didn’t do receipts and that kind of civil matter,” Dupré said. “He painted five paintings and then spent them on alcohol, drugs and women. He wasn’t really businesslike.”

As to the painting now part of the Rijks collection, Dupré says: “Have you ever had an envelope from the Tax and Customs Administration?… He deliberately painted those two people’s sweaters in exactly the same colour.”

As for the gun? “Everyone would want to have that in their hand when you get a tax assessment, right?” Dupré told AD.

Great honour

“He would have thought this was a great honour,” Brood’s wife Xandra Brood told the AD, adding that she had to point out colours to him because the artist was colour-blind. “He worked very fast and made several paintings one after the other.”

She hopes the painting will eventually hang on the walls of Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, his greatest wish.

This painting’s estimated value is 13,000 to 15,000 euros, but Dupré says that’s maybe gone up 50% since the painting became part of the national collection Thursday.

That inclusion, says Dupré, is official recognition of the artist’s craftsmanship. “He was much more than a side-working rock star. And that is now being recognised.”

World.title: French customs seize thousands of THC sweets bound for NL
World.content:
French customs officers have intercepted 3,560 packs of cannabis-laced sweets that were being shipped from the US to the Netherlands, the European anti-fraud office OLAF said on Thursday.

The sweets contained THC, the main psychoactive substance in cannabis. Of the packs, 3,213 copied the look of a “very well-known European gummy brand”, using altered lettering to resemble its name. OLAF did not name the brand. All the packs have been destroyed.

OLAF did not say who the sweets were meant to be delivered to in the Netherlands.

In a statement, the agency said the familiar packaging gives the false impression of an ordinary, safe product, but that a single product could contain a high amount of THC, and children could be at risk.

Cannabis sweets have caused several scares in the Netherlands. This summer, Utrecht police warned parents after two children became ill from sweets found in a school playground, broadcaster NOS reported.

World.title: Seven Rotterdam police officers to face trial over arrest death
World.content:
Seven police officers will go on trial in January next year over the death of a 32-year-old man who was held in a “prone position” on the ground for a long time after being tasered during an arrest in Rotterdam in 2023, the public prosecution department (OM) said on Thursday.

Two officers chased the man on June 9 that year, first in a police van and then on foot, after reports that he had crashed his bicycle into a car and then cycled on.

When he ignored their instructions, one officer used a taser, but it did not incapacitate him or stop him from further resisting. More officers arrived and several of them pinned him down. Soon after he became unwell and was given CPR but died in hospital.

In February 2024 the OM said it would prosecute eight officers after an investigation by the Rijksrecherche, which investigates the police. A pathologist concluded the man’s death could have been caused by the way he was restrained.

The officers are accused of breaching the rules on the use of force with fatal consequences, which has been a criminal offence in its own right since July 2022.

The OM said on Thursday it had dropped a case against an eighth officer, as he was still in training and was following instructions.

The case will be heard on January 19 and from February 15 to 18 by the Blauwe Kamer, a special court in Utrecht that handles cases against police officers. The court will rule on all seven cases at the same time.

In September another Rotterdam man, Alfredo Goeloe (51), died during an arrest after collapsing while officers held him on the ground. That incident led to protests in the city. The Rijksrecherche is investigating his death as well.

World.title: Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis. However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters. On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw. At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors. The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her. Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”. Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”. Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”. ⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94 — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026 The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal. Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence. At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker. The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners. Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki. Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”. On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki. @PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute. Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026 Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted. On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”. Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki. “One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Chaos at Poland’s constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki. One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool. Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw. Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego. Policja nie chce go przepuścić! Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3 — Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026 The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening. On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered. The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence. However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK. “I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.” Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026 Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański. He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”. That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties. She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio. Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995. 🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia” – sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026 While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added. Nastąpiło bezprawne przejęcie strony internetowej Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Prezesem @TK_GOV_PL jest nadal Bogdan Święczkowski, a Wiceprezesem Bartłomiej Sochański. Pani Anna Korwin-Piotrowska nie jest sędzią Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Wszystkie osoby uczestniczące w… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) October 30, 2026 The court’s spokeswoman, Weronika Ścibor, told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “seven people elected as [TK] judges this year” had been escorted into the building by officers from the State Protection Service (SOP), a body responsible for protecting state officials. SOP is subordinate to the interior minister. She said they had entered the grounds of the court through a gate that leads from the prime minister’s chancellery, rather than the main entrance from the street where protesters are gathered. Korwin-Piotrowska also confirmed to TVP that she was one of seven judges who were inside the TK on Friday evening. Rzeczniczka Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Weronika Ścibor komentuje sytuację w TK. Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026 The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński declared outside the court that “as of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism”. Kaczyński called on Nawrocki to return to Poland from his state visit to Senegal and defend the court. The president himself quickly confirmed that he had done so, with flight trackers showing his plane turning around in midair and heading back to Poland. Meanwhile, Zbigniew Kapiński, the chief justice of the Supreme Court – a separate entity from the Constitutional Tribunal – told Kanał Zero that he was “appalled” by what was happening, which was “undoubtedly a coup d’état”. Our most tracked flight right now: A Polish government aircraft en route to Senegal is now returning to Warsaw. https://t.co/YdLhQmV8pl pic.twitter.com/Dz9KPgI3eI — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 30, 2026 Tusk, however, issued a statement on social media defending what was taking place at the TK. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland approves first fast-track renewable energy zones
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity. The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures. The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years. Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆 ❓Czym jest OPRO? ✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich… — Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026 Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly. Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days. The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels. Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”. The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly. Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects. EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late. Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU. However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish Left seeks to end state funding of clergy’s social contributions as government reform stalls
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Left, a junior partner in Poland’s ruling coalition, has proposed a bill to abolish the Church Fund, which provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy. It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund. However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted. 📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️ Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️ ✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026 The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings. It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty. Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half. For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.” At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found. In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025 An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained. Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law. “I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”. Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge. In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled. Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed. Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners. A long-term decline in trust in the Catholic church in Poland has accelerated over the last year, with only 35% of Poles now saying they trust the church. Meanwhile, the armed forces now enjoy record-high trust of 94% https://t.co/ErCBE4HwWR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 17, 2025 Religious communities also criticised the proposal for not having been discussed with them in advance. In a press statement sent to PAP, the Polish Episcopal Conference (KEP), the main organ of the Catholic church in Poland, said any solution should comply with the country’s agreement with the Vatican, as well as the constitutional principle that relations between the state and religious communities be regulated by mutual agreement. Bishop Jerzy Samiec, head of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland, the country’s biggest Protestant body, pointed to the significant costs churches face in maintaining their properties, including care homes and other facilities. The Catholic Church, Poland’s dominant religious institution, has seen a long-term decline in public trust, with only 35% of Poles saying they trusted it in 2025. That has coincided with a series of crises in recent years, in particular over revelations of child sexual abuse by members of the clergy and negligence in dealing with them by the church hierarchy. A variety of surveys, including from the church itself, show that religious attendance and identification have been declining in Poland in recent years. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition leader sparks controversy with speech on potential EU exit talks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, has sparked controversy by appearing to suggest that Poland and some other allied European Union member states could launch the process of leaving the EU if they fail in efforts to reform it. His remarks were condemned by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and other figures from the pro-EU ruling coalition, who have long accused Kaczyński and his national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party of seeking “Polexit” from the EU. However, Kaczyński responded by accusing Tusk of misrepresenting his words, insisting that he wants Poland to reform the EU rather than leave it. Kaczyński pomylił Krynicę z Kremlem. pic.twitter.com/tX0G04krze — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) October 29, 2026 The comments in question came in an hour-long speech by Kaczyński at the Krynica Forum, an annual conference bringing together leaders from politics, business and civil society, which he used to outline his vision for sweeping reforms of the EU. Repeating his longstanding criticism of Brussels, Kaczyński warned that there had been a “consistent drive to transform the EU into a centralised state” with too much power over national governments. He also called the European Parliament in its current form a “parody”. But soon, said Kaczyński, “a window of opportunity” for reform may appear because “completely different governments could emerge” in Poland, France and Spain, all of which will hold elections within the year. PiS has previously enjoyed close relations with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party in France and the nationalist Vox party of Santiago Abascal in Spain. The EU is preparing a "German plan" that would "annihilate the Polish state", said Kaczyński as Poland marks Independence Day. He warned that the incoming opposition government will "strive to implement this plan" and called on Poles to "fight" against it https://t.co/QDbxmiaazJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2023 Kaczyński suggested that Poland, if led by PiS, could work with other like-minded EU governments to push for reform of the bloc by influencing public opinion, identifying breaches of EU treaties, creating a blocking minority in the European Council, and trying to change the EU’s treaties. However, the PiS leader then warned that, “if [those] approaches fail to yield results, the states that want change could conclude a new treaty with the elements we are seeking, but with a delayed entry into force”. Kaczyński then noted that the EU treaties “include provisions specifying the terms under which a state may withdraw from the EU. This all begins with negotiations. And simply begin these negotiations”. “It is a tough approach, a risky one, but the situation is so dire that it is worth employing such a method if all others fail to yield results,” he added. The remarks immediately prompted condemnation from figures in Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused Kaczyński of effectively calling for Polexit – something they have long claimed he wants, even though PiS has not explicitly called for it before. “Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the terms of its withdrawal from the EU,” wrote Tusk himself on X. “This is, among other things, what the current struggle in Poland is about – a tough struggle. I do not intend to lose it.” “So they do want Polexit after all,” wrote foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Customs borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania…An end to subsidies for farmers and investments…And they swore on their lives that they’d never do that.” In a video published later on Thursday, Tusk declared that next year’s parliamentary elections would help decide “whether Poland remains in the European Union or leaves it”. Jarosław Kaczyński ogłosił właśnie, że Polska powinna zacząć rokowania o warunkach wyjścia z Unii Europejskiej. O taką między innymi stawkę toczy się dziś w Polsce walka. Twarda walka. Nie zamierzam jej przegrać, nawet jeśli nie wszyscy zagrają ze mną. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 29, 2026 Kaczyński responded by saying that “Tusk is lying as usual”. He emphasised that he believes “the EU is needed but it requires thorough reform” so that it “benefits not the elites, but ordinary citizens”. PiS deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek said on Thursday that his party was “considering all scenarios, including the possibility that the EU will kill itself”. However, he added that the priority remained reforming the bloc and “PiS has no plans to leave the EU”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). When PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it regularly clashed with Brussels over a variety of issues, including judicial reform, trade, climate policy, and migration. Since Tusk, a former president of the European Council, took power in 2023, his government has greatly improved relations with Brussels. Tusk jak zwykle kłamie. Najwyraźniej wychodzi z założenia, że dzień bez kłamstwa jest dniem straconym… Unia Europejska jest potrzebna, ale wymaga gruntownej reformy. Kryzys i zapaść w jej obecnym kształcie to efekt rządów Merkel i jednego z jej pomocników, Tuska. Nie ma co się… — Jarosław Kaczyński (@OficjalnyJK) October 29, 2026 Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU funding since joining the bloc in 2004. A study published earlier this year found that the country’s economy is 42% larger than it would have been had Poland not been part of the EU. Opinion polls consistently show a large majority of Poles in favour of remaining part of the EU. However, recent years have seen an uptick in support for Polexit, as well as for anti-EU far-right parties. PiS has increasingly found itself competing against such parties for votes. Regular polling by state research agency CBOS shows that, while opposition to EU membership fell to a record low of 5% in 2022, it has subsequently risen, standing at 14% in the most recent survey. World.title: Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
