At a secondary school in the village of Hlushkivka, in the Kupiansk district, investigators found not only Russian textbooks and tricolor flags but also posters featuring Russian literary figures. Among them were Gogol and Shevchenko. The caption beneath Shevchenko read: “Poet, prose writer, artist. Bought out of serfdom by Russians. Kept his diary in Russian.”

Shevchenko’s monuments in Melitopol and Balakliia

In January 2023, Russian occupying forces removed a monument to Taras Shevchenko from the center of occupied Melitopol, in the Zaporizhzhia region. The dismantling took place late in the evening. The city’s mayor, Ivan Fedorov, reported the removal, adding: “They probably took him to the basement. That’s the only way they know how to deal with those they don’t like.”

He knew about basements from personal experience. In March 2022, he was abducted from his office, a bag was pulled over his head, and a week later he was exchanged for nine very young Russian conscripts captured by Ukrainian forces. By May 9, 2025, a bust of Stalin had been installed on the pedestal in Melitopol where Shevchenko’s monument had stood.

Shevchenko has repeatedly reappeared in Ukrainian territories soon after Russian forces were driven out. A short video, filmed by Ukrainian Air Force assault troops in the liberated city of Balakliia, in the Kharkiv region, during the autumn 2023 counteroffensive, was shown on what seemed like every television channel in the country.

In the footage, soldiers tear down a Russian tricolor banner from a roadside billboard. It bears the words “We are one people with Russia.” Beneath it, a portrait of the Kobzar is revealed, along with a famous stanza from his poem The Caucasus. The banner had been put up in the last year before the invasion that could still be described as relatively peaceful, to mark another anniversary of Ukraine’s independence.

One soldier reacts in disbelief: “Holy f—!” Another orders him: “Read it!” And he reads the stanza aloud:

“Fight on – and you will prevail! God is with you! For you are truth, for you are glory, and holy freedom!”

Serhiy Nihoyan, a student who became one of the first people killed during the Maidan protests, had recited the same passage aloud against a backdrop of barricades.

Today, in Kyiv’s Lukianivka district, where little remains untouched, a banner bearing Shevchenko’s portrait and the words “We are fighting. We will prevail” covers the facade of a damaged building. Ukrainians immediately recognize the reference: the call to “Fight on – and you will prevail!” is etched into their collective memory.

Shevchenko’s lines are continually adapted to the moment. At Barbara, a coffee shop near the author’s home, one version reads: “Get out of our home. We are free forever. There will be no Muscovy here. Glory to Ukraine!”

Chernecha hill under the tsars

The hill near Kaniv, overlooking the Dnipro River and its green slopes, became a place of pilgrimage almost immediately after Shevchenko’s remains were transferred there from St. Petersburg in May 1861, in accordance with his Testament.

In 1884, local residents raised funds to erect a cast-iron cross. Nearby, at the edge of the woods, they built a simple hut.

One half became an improvised folk museum called Tarasova Svitlytsia (“Taras’s Chamber”); the other served as the home of a caretaker. The exhibits included a copy of Kobzar, an oil portrait of the poet with a halo above his head, brushes belonging to an unknown artist, a kobza, a traditional Ukrainian stringed instrument, and an old visitors’ book lying on a table.

Embroidered Ukrainian towels, known as rushnyky, hung on the walls, including some bearing Shevchenko’s image. Many of those who brought them could neither read nor write, yet knew his poems by heart.

Secret reports from the Kaniv gendarmerie on visitors to the site have survived in the State Archives of the Kyiv Region. People came to Chernecha Hill not only from neighboring villages but from far away. Surveillance intensified ahead of major anniversaries.

The authorities refused to permit either accommodation for pilgrims or the establishment of an association to maintain and protect the grave. A document dated April 8, 1910, from the Kyiv provincial authority responsible for public associations explained why. Such an association, it warned, “would provide a convenient means of bringing together activists and adherents of the Ukrainophile party, allowing them to gather in an isolated place, difficult for the administration to observe and monitor.”

The association’s activities, officials cautioned, “would be directed toward strengthening propaganda for the cultural and political autonomy of Little Russia.” They even found evidence of suspicious intentions in the application’s failure to specify the language to be used for official business. The implication was clear: the language in question might not be Russian.

The Moscow art theatre at Shevchenko’s grave

The warnings from the gendarmerie and the authorities’ fears of “advocates of autonomy” did not deter prominent figures in Russia’s artistic and intellectual circles.

Zinaida Tarakhan-Bereza, the oldest living staff member of the Shevchenko National Reserve, cites historical accounts in her scholarly chronicle The Shrine (Kyiv, 1998). In May 1912, a steamer decorated with Shevchenko’s portrait, embroidered towels and flowers arrived at the Kaniv landing.

“No speeches, politically charged songs or other demonstrative performances!” the “tourists” were reminded once again as they came ashore.

Only two wreaths were permitted at the poet’s grave.

One came from the Ukrainian Club, a national and cultural association headed by the composer Mykola Lysenko. The other was an elaborate wrought-metal wreath decorated with oak leaves, symbolizing eternity, a laurel branch and a bronze plaque bearing the inscription: “A bow to the ground before the genius Shevchenko from the Moscow Art Theatre.”

The Moscow Art Theatre was touring Kyiv at the time. From then on, its actors spent every summer living communally at a nearby hamlet beside Taras Hill, drawing inspiration from the place. Among them were Ivan Moskvin, Yevgeny Vakhtangov and Mikhail Chekhov.

The Ukrainian Club was shut down in 1912.

I examined the leaves from the theatre’s wreath in a museum display case. They have survived two world wars and are now enduring Russia’s invasion.

The Museum in a bomb shelter

Few original exhibits remain on display at the museum. The most valuable surviving objects have been moved to a secure location to protect them from bombing.

“Kaniv, and particularly the Kaniv Hydroelectric Power Plant, has come under fire more than once. But our academic council collectively decided not to evacuate anything outside the country,” says Hanna Manzhara, the museum’s senior collections curator.

She is 80 and cannot imagine her life apart from the museum.

“We resumed work in July 2022 because the number of visitors kept growing. That was such an incentive! We moved the exhibition to the basement, which had been converted into a bomb shelter. At the beginning of this year, we returned to the surface, to the galleries.”

Unlike monuments in Kyiv, Shevchenko’s memorial in Kaniv has not been covered with sandbags. It is not simply a sculpture but a burial mound with a crypt inside, a place where people come to pay their respects.

Yet Russian forces have also struck cemeteries: in Cherkasy in July 2025, in Odesa in October 2024 and in Kramatorsk in April 2023.

Hanna Ivanivna Manzhara, senior collections curator. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow

The conversation naturally turns to Russia. The Moscow and St. Petersburg periods of Shevchenko’s life and work cannot simply be erased from his story.

Hanna Manzhara recalls taking part in Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow in 2003, together with Vita Dzyma, a senior researcher.

“The Ukrainian Center on Arbat Street asked us to take part.

“We brought an exhibition featuring lifetime editions of individual poems, as well as publications from 1911 and 1914, marking the 50th anniversaries of his birth and death. We added woven Ukrainian folk towels made by Marуsia Vasylashchuk, a traditional craftswoman. The response was fantastic! Teachers from Moscow came, along with members of the Ukrainian diaspora. Our fellow museum professionals were particularly remarkable in the attention they gave us.”

“And, of course, there were collectors,” Dzyma continues. “I won’t name them; we lost contact a long time ago. But copies of Moscow newspapers reporting on Taras Shevchenko’s funeral found their way to Kaniv through antique shops on Arbat Street.

“The museum was preparing for reconstruction, and we were trying to build up our collection.”

Manzhara adds: “You see, the life and work of the Kobzar are far broader than anything we ourselves could convey to an audience.”

Dzyma has a similar story. In the family of the St. Petersburg literary scholar Ieremiya Aizenshtok, a self-portrait of 16-year-old Taras was discovered, dating from the time he served as Engelhardt’s personal attendant, or kazachok. Research and evidence suggested it was the earliest portrait of the Kobzar.

“But Aizenshtok’s relatives asked for a very high price. The Kaniv museum simply couldn’t afford it. What happened to the portrait, and who owns it now, is unknown.”

At that moment, the author’s phone begins to vibrate: an air-raid alert has been issued in Kyiv.

On social media, Russian military personnel who have spent nearly five years launching missiles, including at Ukrainian museums, are sarcastically dubbed “Pushkinists.” Among the institutions hit have been the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum in Skovorodynivka, the Kupiansk Museum of Local History and the Odesa Fine Arts Museum.

A Shrine to an Icon: The Museum Under Soviet Rule

“Now the working people of Ukraine and the Soviet Union will be able to become more familiar with the great legacy of the poet-revolutionary, a fighter against the social and national oppression that weighed so heavily on the peoples of the former tsarist Russia,” the republican newspaper Kommunist wrote in 1936.

The newspaper recalled that in 1923, a temporary monument had been erected over Shevchenko’s grave “in place of the cross so hated by the poet and all working people,” and that a temporary exhibition had been set up nearby in 1934. At the same time, construction of a museum was underway on Taras Hill.

Visitors often ask why the Soviet authorities invested so heavily in the project during the Holodomor, the famine that devastated Ukraine. It was the first building in Ukraine designed specifically to house a museum. Until then, museums had generally occupied historic aristocratic or manor houses.

Vita Dzyma offers an explanation:

“Look around: every home had a portrait of Shevchenko – embroidered, painted, burned into wood or assembled from straw. Kobzar lay beside the Bible, or took its place when the campaign against religion began.

“The villages at the foot of Taras Hill were being starved to death. People hired themselves out to work on the construction site for a piece of bread. They carried stones by hand, as in ancient Egypt. Yet they were proud of their work. The Shevchenko Museum was no less than a temple.

“Arguing with Ukrainians about this is a losing battle. Taras is both a father and a prophet!”

Vita Dzyma, senior researcher at the museum. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

A sculptural composition of Lenin and Stalin was installed in the entrance hall, while Shevchenko’s bust was moved to the second floor so that it would not compete with them. According to Dzyma, whose account is supported by research, Soviet propagandists in the 1930s seriously pursued the idea of finding a physical resemblance between Lenin and Shevchenko.

The burial mound was given an upgrade, too. Behind a granite balustrade at the base of the monument, a platform was built resembling the speaker’s tribune at Lenin’s Mausoleum, intended for members of the Ukrainian Communist Party’s Politburo.

In 1939, marking the 125th anniversary of the Kobzar’s birth, Nikita Khrushchev, the first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, spoke at the opening of the museum and the unveiling of the new monument.

“The tradition of placing microphones beside Shevchenko and addressing the community as if speaking on his behalf, from his elevated position, has survived to this day,” Hanna Manzhara explains.

The museum under nazi occupation: Director Dmytro Lebedko

In mid-August 1941, the last train carrying mobilized troops left Kaniv across the bridge over the Dnipro. The bridge was bombed, and its ruins can still be seen from Taras Hill.

There was no time to evacuate the museum before the Nazi occupation. Its staff scattered. The women I spoke to avoid going into detail about what happened next. “It would be disrespectful to the local residents,” they say.

Dmytro Lebedko, a former librarian at the reserve who had been mobilized into the Red Army and survived the bombing of his train, found himself in two roles at once: collaborator, having agreed to work with the occupying forces, and preserver of the museum’s collection.

The Nazis did not close the museum. Instead, they ordered it to be put in order and kept open. Visitors, mostly German soldiers, were brought through in formation. For the first time, not a single entry appeared in the visitors’ book.

The local population was afraid to visit Taras Hill, even though in the nearby district center of Horodyshche, the Nazis had toppled a statue of Karl Marx and replaced it with one of Shevchenko.

Archival documents preserve Lebedko’s testimony: “In 1941, I managed to recover from the village of Pekari 15 chairs, about 2,000 books, two carpets embroidered with portraits of Shevchenko, six silk curtains and a number of other valuables.”

After becoming director, he carried out a full inventory of the museum’s collection, cataloguing 4,000 items. He was not afraid to compile a list of paintings and drawings that the local Nazi district commissioner had supposedly taken for “temporary use.” He also recorded every vase and carpet appropriated by yet another official with an interest in “Slavic exoticism.” Then he took a risk that could have cost him his life: he moved the most valuable objects into a hiding place, sealed it behind a wall and went into hiding himself.

After Soviet troops arrived, Lebedko still managed to help restore the museum, which the Nazis had ransacked shortly before retreating. He voluntarily admitted in court to having been involved in a “Ukrainian nationalist Bandera organization.”

The authorities demanded that he strengthen his self-incriminating statement. “I thought Soviet rule would no longer exist in Ukraine and that Ukraine would become independent. I now understand the serious political error in my views,” he was made to say.

He was convicted of treason and sentenced to the maximum term. Three years later, he died in the Norilsk labor camps from a perforated stomach ulcer.

Dmytro Lebedko was 47, the same age as Taras Shevchenko. His name was erased from the history of the reserve for decades. Museum staff emphasize that only 10 exhibits from the prewar collection have survived to this day.

Yanukovych’s makeover

Toward the end of Leonid Kuchma’s presidency, plans emerged for a major restoration project in Kaniv. A nationwide fund was established specifically to restore historical and architectural heritage sites, and UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya, a Ukrainian research and design institute specializing in restoration, was selected to develop the project. Its specialists proposed returning the building to its original appearance, based on the drawings of architect Vasyl Krychevsky.

In the 1930s, Krychevsky had been unable to realize his full vision. His design was deemed “too Ukrainian,” and both he and his closest student, Petro Kostyrko, were removed from the project. The construction was completed by more compliant hands. As a result, museum staff, whose building had received no major restoration since World War II, were afraid even to express their hopes aloud.

The project stalled, then resumed under President Viktor Yanukovych. According to those involved, the massive, even pompous building made a strong impression on him. If the museum was to host the annual Shevchenko National Prize ceremony, Ukraine’s highest state award for achievements in culture and the arts, it had to meet the president’s aesthetic standards.

Few understood Yanukovych’s tastes better than Hanna Herman, one of his closest allies, a member of parliament from the Party of Regions and head of its humanitarian policy team, and her protégé, architect Larysa Skoryk.

“History repeated itself,” Vita Dzyma says. “At the final stage, UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya was removed from the project, and the national character of the design was discarded. ‘No painted decoration on the exterior – this isn’t some village hut!’ they said. But the preparatory work for the majolica facade had already been completed. The same was true of the alfresco work – the decorative painting in relief.

“The Ministry of Culture’s scientific and methodological council convened and decided: whitewash it!”

Hanna Manzhara adds: “Even the surviving fragments of Krychevsky’s original work, which had miraculously survived the previous war and were rediscovered during the restoration, were covered up again.”

Skoryk developed a stripped-down design concept. The polychrome landscape inspired by the poem Haidamaky was replaced with a monochrome version.

The original coffered ceiling was concealed behind a stretch ceiling. Red lines of Shevchenko’s poetry ran across the gray fabric like information scrolling through a subway station. Glass replaced the wooden mosaic partitions in the entrance hall, while granite slabs took the place of parquet flooring.

“We wanted at least to restore the unique botanical and floral patterns on the columns.

“Both museum staff and Krychevsky’s relatives wrote to Yanukovych. It made no difference. What we got was a gray-and-white renovation,” Dzyma concludes.

She asks whether the author noticed the granite boulder at the entrance, in the center of the lobby. The author is puzzled. Surely this is not a geological museum.

▇ “Shevchenko is the cornerstone of the national idea. It’s a metaphor!”

Photographs From 1944 and a Forced-Labor Camp in the Museum

The author’s attention was drawn to two framed photographs on the wall, dated the last day of January 1944. Yakov Davidzon, a frontline correspondent, arrived at Taras Hill immediately after Kaniv was liberated. He found the museum surrounded by barbed wire, with burned books, torn paintings and shattered sculptures. Sixteen shrapnel wounds had been counted on the pedestal of Shevchenko’s monument.

“We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section.

She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup.

Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death.

Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner?

The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region:

“We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!”

Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka

In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling.

The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum.

The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar.

“There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged.

“In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.”

More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission.

Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced.

“We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls.

The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran.

In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world.

The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda

“Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.

“The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’

“They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’

“To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.”

“The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues.

Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.”

The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve.

Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian.

Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity.

But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance.

World.title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
World.content:
TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies

Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation.

The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies.

Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed.

Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service.

According to the list published by Transparency International Georgia, the officials named include:

Merab Bekaia – deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +.

– deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +. Nino Vashakidze – deputy head of Tbilisi City Hall’s Property Management Agency and director of two private companies, Bidara and Il Gudauri.

– head of the Foreign Ministry’s International Economic Relations Department and director of private company Kospot. Shota Andriadze – deputy director of the state-run Municipal Development Fund and director of private company Aipi.

– deputy head of the National Wine Agency and director of private company Wine Events and Consulting. Temur Gasviani – deputy minister of justice and civic integration of the Autonomous Republic of Abkhazia and director of private company Strada.

Irakli Dzadzamia – deputy chair of the ruling Georgian Dream party faction in Tsalenjikha Municipal Council and director of private company Global Construction Group.

– deputy chair of the ruling Georgian Dream party faction in Tsalenjikha Municipal Council and director of private company Global Construction Group. Nodar Asatiani – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Tskaltubo Municipal Council and director of private company Asani Construction.

– head of Bolnisi City Hall’s Spatial Planning and Infrastructure Department and director of two private companies, G and N Business Group and Pagi. Solomon Gorashvili – head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani.

– head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani. Roland Abuladze – head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative.

– head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative. Bidzina Mekvevrishvili – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Akhmeta Municipal Council and head of the Magraani agricultural cooperative.

What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Azerbaijani wrestler wins bronze medal at World Championships
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. Azerbaijani freestyle wrestler Ali Tsokayev has won the bronze medal at the World Wrestling Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan.

Competing in the 92kg weight category, the Azerbaijani wrestler faced Iran’s Amirhossein Firouzpour Bandpei in the bronze medal bout.

Tsokayev defeated his opponent 6-0 to secure a place on the podium.

With this result, Azerbaijan’s medal tally at the tournament has reached six. The national team has won two gold, two silver and two bronze medals.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s industrial output rises 7% to $7.83B in nine months
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. Kyrgyzstan’s industrial output from January through September 2026 totaled 685.4 billion soms ($7.83 billion), up 7% in physical terms from a year earlier, the National Statistical Committee said.

Growth came from higher output in several manufacturing industries and in mining.

Chemical production rose 2.3 times and refined oil products 1.9 times. Wood and paper products and printing grew 41.3%, motor vehicles 39.4%, construction materials 29.1% and pharmaceuticals 13.6%.

Food, beverages and tobacco rose 9.4% and mining 7.3%. The committee also reported growth in electricity, gas and steam supply, linked to higher distribution of electricity and gas.

Industry grew much more slowly than construction, where output rose 1.6 times to 380 billion soms. Agricultural output rose 6.5% to 399.5 billion soms ($4.57 billion).

According to Trend’s analysis, Kyrgyzstan’s industrial sector could sustain positive growth through the end of 2026, supported by expanding chemical production, refined petroleum products, construction materials, food processing and mining.

However, the pace of expansion may moderate as the sector faces a higher comparison base and uneven performance across industries. Industrial output growth slowed from 8.8% in January–August 2026 to 7% in January–September, a decline of 1.8 percentage points in the cumulative year-on-year growth rate. The World Bank’s October 2026 economic outlook also points to continued economic expansion, while identifying higher fuel prices and production costs as risks to activity.

World.title: France opens 'attempted murder' probe after riot police attacked with petrol bomb
World.content:
French prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation into rioters who threw a petrol bomb at police during protests in Paris on Saturday.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including high school and university students, staged a third weekend of demonstrations in the French capital and other parts of the country over education and living costs.

While mostly peaceful, some gatherings in Paris ended in "extraordinary" levels of violence from some rioters, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.

Rioters have been accused of targeting police with projectiles during the third weekend of France's protests. (Reuters: Pedro Nunes)

The Paris Police Prefecture accused several hundred rioters of attacking security forces with projectiles, including a molotov cocktail.

"Explosive devices were thrown at around fifteen gendarmes as well as police officers," the prosecutor's office said on Sunday.

Gendarmes are the military police branch of the French armed forces. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country on Saturday to respond to an estimated 320,000 protesters nationwide.

Prosecutors said an investigation had been opened in Paris for "attempted murder of persons vested with public authority".

Unpacking the European protests Footage of mass protests in Europe has been flooding newsfeeds for weeks, with demonstrators taking to the streets across the continent.

Video and photos from a gathering in the city's east showed an incendiary device exploding at the feet of police.

Prosecutors on Sunday said initial injuries included second-degree burns.

The gendarme struck by the Molotov cocktail told French television of the burns he suffered, describing "skin that stings" and a "rain" of projectiles thrown at his unit.

Investigators are working to identify those responsible, with no suspects in custody, the prosecutor's office said.

Fewer shops damaged

Loading...

More than 770 people were arrested during weekend protests in France, the interior ministry said on Sunday.

The ministry said there had been "no major incidents" late on Saturday.

The number of shops damaged on the sidelines of Saturday's protests was significantly lower than previous weekends, with some 20 businesses affected, according to France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

But CCI France voiced concern about the impact of protests on retail activity ahead of the peak year-end holiday season.

School blockades to restart Monday

Demonstrations in Paris remained peaceful for hours before clashes broke out towards the end. (Reuters: Abdul Saboor)

France's protests emerged from weeks of demonstrations by high school students protesting deteriorating learning conditions and inequality.

Efforts from the French government to address concerns have largely failed to appease student protesters.

Pierre Sourzat, head of the "Lyceens!" student group, said high school blockades would restart from Monday when students return from a two-week holiday.

"It will be more significant from Tuesday, but we know that some schools will be blocked as early as tomorrow," he told French broadcaster RMC.

"We support all our comrades who are blocking their schools from tomorrow."

Proposed government measures aimed at addressing students' demands, include replacing the university admissions platform and providing loans for school renovations.

Troops deployed and curfews implemented to quell France riots A massive security operation will be in place ahead of planned protests this weekend, ministers have said.

But students do not believe the proposals go far enough.

On Saturday, Sabrine Kharbach, spokeswoman for the Union Etudiante (Student Union), said blockades of universities and high schools would take place on Tuesday and Thursday.

President Emmanuel Macron has called for classes to resume in a calm manner, arguing that "young people have been heard".

Mr Sourzat countered, saying "the president hasn't listened to us".

"It's smoke and mirrors," he said.

"There's a bit of polish on the surface, but once you scratch beneath it, there's nothing there."

Mr Sourzat said the proposed overhaul of the university admissions platform, long criticised for its lack of transparency, failed to address the shortage of places in higher education.

He also dismissed the government's plan to reduce class sizes as insufficient, noting that it would apply only to 10th-grade classes.

"We were asking for all year groups," he said.

AFP

World.title: Australia nears 'largest property downturn in 40 years' as prices plunge
World.content:
National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years, according to property research group Cotality.

Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling.

The index shows the median national house price now stands at $884,855.

Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said the speed of decline was tracking faster than any previous downturn over the past 40 years, with capital city values down 8.1 per cent in seven months.

Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in values over the past three months as buyers struggle to get loans because of higher interest rates.

It sits alongside investor demand also waning because of the federal government's budget changes to property tax breaks.

"This is really a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said.

"That's reduced the borrowing capacity of households, but also increased the repayments for people to make on a mortgage, and it's pushed a lot of buyers to the side."

Gerard Burg says house prices will fall further. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Mr Burg is among many economists anticipating higher rates for longer and further house price falls.

"We are already on track to see the largest downturn across the last 40 years," he said.

"The previous record was 2017 through 2019, which stood at 8.2 per cent [falls] across the combined capital cities. Now, at the moment, as of October, the downturn that we've seen over the past seven months is 8.1 per cent [falls], so it looks like we're easily going to push past that mark."

How much further will house prices fall?

The number of home sales has dropped sharply as demand weakens.

Cotality puts the number of home sales over the past three months 23 per cent lower than a year ago and 18 per cent below the previous five-year average.

With fewer buyers, it has become harder to sell homes. Auction clearance rates across the combined capitals are consistently tracking below 50 per cent, while private treaty metrics have also weakened.

The median time on market, at 39 days, is the highest since August 2020, while vendor discounting, at 4.7 per cent, is the largest since May 2019.

Mr Burg said buyers would hold back until the Reserve Bank of Australia indicated a different direction on rates, and that likely would not happen until the latter half of 2027.

"The eventual recovery that we do see in the housing market is likely to be more subdued than we've seen in previous episodes," Mr Burg said.

"It [the RBA] doesn't necessarily require rates to come down, but [give] the clear signal that that is the direction that they are going to take."

Domain's chief economist Nicola Powell says it could be well into next year before rate cuts are on the agenda.

"We've already seen about a 6 per cent shave from the median house price, so the reality is a 10 per cent drop in price is quite possible," Ms Powell said.

"We need something to change to improve buyer confidence. And that isn't going to come at least until we have the discussion of a potential rate cut. And that's unlikely to happen until the latter part of 2027."

Nicola Powell says it could be well into next year before rate cuts are on the agenda. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Inquiries at some open homes down 300 pc

Harcourts real estate agent and auctioneer Sam Devlin, who sells homes in Brisbane, said over the past six months enquiries at open homes had been down in some instances by 300 per cent.

"That's been brought on since the May budget," he said.

"The government's taxation policies around negative gearing and capital gains tax have certainly affected what is happening there."

Sam Devlin sells homes in Brisbane but is seeing fewer buyers. (ABC News: Ben Cocklin)

Mr Devlin said even buyers looking to upsize were heading to auctions unsure whether they could stump up the cash.

"Right now, we're seeing a real lack of confidence from people who have to sell homes, being able to transact without subject to sale clauses," he said.

"There would be more interest if there was more confidence in the market that buyers could actually sell the house that they're already in."

Jin Ling at real estate agent Vic Prop sells homes in Melbourne's eastern suburbs. He said enquiries were down and buyers were far more cautious.

"Right now, they don't have the confidence that, if rates go up two or three more times over the next 12 months, whether that's a comfortable position for them," he said.

" They're thinking, 'Do we wait 12 months? Do we wait to see what the market does? Do we wait for prices to maybe potentially pull back a bit more before kind of pulling the trigger? "

Mr Ling said it could take years for property values to rise strongly again.

"I think it'll be a three-to-four-year period, where hopefully we can see a level of recovery," Mr Ling said.

Jin Ling says enquiries are down and buyers are far more cautious. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Property bargains for some?

In the meantime, some buyers could get better value.

House prices fall for sixth month Australian house prices have fallen for a sixth month in a row.

Recent data from Domain showed Melbourne was just $14,000 away from the median house price falling below $1 million.

Cotality's data is modelled differently and already had Melbourne well below that. Its October figures show Melbourne's median dwelling price is $773,027.

"We've seen the upper end of our markets, particularly in Sydney and Melbourne, see price falls for a much longer period of time. Those price falls were happening at the end of 2025," Domain chief economist Nicola Powell said.

" It can create opportunities for some types of buyers, particularly those looking to upsize, because you tend to find the upper end, so the more expensive the property is, the deeper the price falls. "

House prices continue to fall in major cities across Australia. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Ling said he had already seen greater buyer interest from people living interstate for homes in Melbourne.

"Previously, it was Melbourne investors going, 'Hey, you know [we are looking at] buying in Perth, buying in Brisbane, buying in Adelaide. And I think now [that's] reversed," Mr Ling said.

He said for all the dire predictions, there was going to be greater value for those looking to buy their first home or wishing to upsize.

"I think that there are incredible buying opportunities out there," he said.

World.title: One in four young men now say violence for a cause can be justified
World.content:
One in four young men say "extreme measures", such as violence, can sometimes be justified to advance a cause, according to new research tracking Australians' views on democracy.

The second McKinnon Index, released today, also shows trust in politicians and government has fallen compared to last year, while almost three-quarters of Australians believe the country is more divided than 12 months ago.

More than 4,000 Australians were surveyed on their attitudes towards democracy, led by the not-for-profit organisation McKinnon and conducted with Roy Morgan in June and July this year.

The results have been released amid a broader conversation about political safety and the state of Australian democracy after an alleged attack on Independent MP Helen Haines near her parliamentary office in regional Victoria last month. An alleged motive in that incident remains unknown.

The survey finds that Australians largely support democracy, with more than three quarters still saying it is preferable to any other system of government.

Support for democracy slides for young men

Some of the largest movements in the data occurred for men aged 18 to 24.

There was an increase in the proportion of young men who said extreme measures could sometimes be justified, rising to more than 27 per cent.

That compares to one in 10 across the whole population, while more than three-quarters of Australians disagreed.

Support for democracy also declined among young men to 54 per cent, while there was a sharp 23-point drop in the proportion who believed people could freely express political opinions, to about 50 per cent.

McKinnon interim executive chairman and former Victorian deputy premier John Thwaites said it was important to acknowledge that while those who said violence could be justified in some circumstances were in the minority, it was an increasing proportion.

"We need to do more to ensure that all of our community, but young men here in particular, understand our democracy, understand the importance of it, and understand that their voice is important and can be heard," he said.

McKinnon's John Thwaites says the research shows the connection between the public and politicians is under pressure. (ABC News)

Confidence in politics drops in regional areas

The survey more broadly showed Australians were less satisfied with democracy, with fewer than half believing the political system gave people like them a say.

Those who said they had low trust in the federal government cited broken promises, dishonesty and politicians being out of touch as the most common reasons.

The trend was more pronounced for people with lower education levels and those who lived in the regions.

In inner regional areas, dissatisfaction in democracy rose to nearly 39 per cent, higher than the national proportion of about 30 per cent.

Cathy McGowan, who was the Independent MP for Indi before Ms Haines, said people in rural and regional Australia were bearing the brunt of inequality.

But she said since the alleged attack on Ms Haines, she has heard calls all over Australia "for us to be better and do better".

"There's also a role for community to be much more active in holding each other to account and creating the environment that they want to protect the democracy that they value."

Helen Haines won the seat of Indi following Cathy McGowan's retirement, making history as the first independent to succeed another. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Trust in the public service is steady

While trust in politicians and governments has declined, faith in public servants and democratic institutions has largely remained steady or increased.

Nearly half of Australians said they trusted the federal public service, while satisfaction in the education system and public infrastructure also rose.

The Australian Electoral Commission had the highest trust level, with more than 70 per cent, followed by government regulators and advisory bodies at 57 per cent and the courts at 55 per cent.

University of Melbourne political science associate professor Aaron Martin said he had observed similar trends in his own research, including that support for institutions like the electoral commission remained high for the most part.

While he said it was difficult to read a trend from the two years of data provided by the McKinnon Index, other studies like the Australian Election Study showed satisfaction with democracy had risen between the 2019 and 2025 federal elections.

"I think over the longer term, the picture is a little more optimistic than the sort of snapshots that we're getting at the moment," he said.

Threats against MPs rising The attack on Helen Haines comes amid a rise in threats of political violence.

Dr Martin said globally Australia sat between countries doing "really badly", such as the US, the UK, France and Spain, and countries doing "really well", like Denmark.

"Australia is in a pretty reasonable position, but that's not to say that we're in a sort of unassailable position either," he said.

Mr Thwaites said leaders needed to take note of the loss of trust.

"People need to know their voice matters. They also need to see leaders acting with integrity, keeping their promises and delivering outcomes that make a difference to their lives."

World.title: Tonga and Samoa can be State of Origin for the new century
World.content:
It's not often you can feel when history is happening right around you but that is what happens when Samoa meets Tonga.

The two island nations met in the most eagerly anticipated clash of the Rugby League World Cup and in the end it was Tonga who claimed the honours with a 20-18 victory.

It sets up two classic semi-finals, where Samoa will play Australia and Tonga take on New Zealand, but that feels secondary to what happened at Parramatta on Sunday.

It took everything Tonga had and then it took a little more, with the result in the balance until the final minute of a contest that was fuelled by the power of the past and teased a golden vision of tomorrow.

As State of Origin once changed the sport by creating matches that feel as big as rugby league ever can, games like this prove Samoa and Tonga can do the same.

It can be the Origin of the new century, a rivalry without end that makes itself anew every year as a date every fan — Samoan, Tongan and otherwise, rusted-on and casual — can circle on the calendar as one of rugby league's biggest nights.

It can fill stadiums as easily as it does hearts. The crowd for this one was the highest for any sporting event at the new Parramatta Stadium and would have eclipsed last year's Lang Park total of 45,000 if only the place was bigger.

It was a mighty occasion between Tonga and Samoa in Parramatta. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It draws in eyeballs, demands attention and adds zeroes to television deals — which means it can turn a profit, In a world where games are reduced to content on a balance sheet, that alone makes the case for more.

This was a match that delivered on its promises of blood and fire and speed and craft, and it was right that it felt timeless because rugby league is just the newest framework for something that has been happening for centuries.

What happens on the field and in the stands is the expression of a relationship that has existed between Tonga and Samoa since before either had written word.

It was already old when the colonisers came, and there are moments you can feel its power so fully and clearly you may as well be able to reach out and touch it.

It was in the steel eyes of Tim Lafai, the retired Samoan legend who grew up in a house with walls, as he led the team out dressed in traditional garb.

It was in the sound of the anthems, the notes that rose and the tears that flowed and the flags that flew, and the carnivore roaring of the cultural challenges.

It was in the ferocious tackling, as both teams dished out hits that would scare a starving dog off a meat truck. Just watching was enough to wake up with bruises in the morning.

Jarome Luai's effort to fight well out of his weight class and pop Demitric Vaimauga was the pick of a brutal bunch but Vaimauga's own effort on Spencer Leniu in the second half was near as thunderous.

Most of all, it was in the way this game felt like it was on the edge of a knife as time ran down.

Both teams were bound to play again next week, but for brief moments it seemed like tomorrow wouldn't exist for whoever end up on the wrong end of things — because they would not lose a game, but a part of themselves.

Samoa's speed put them ahead, and they seemed to be riding home the stronger, only for Tonga's power to show one last time as Addin Fonua-Blake snake-hipped past Leniu for the winning try.

A rematch in the World Cup final is possible, even as both teams are likely outsiders, but regardless this has to happen again soon. People want this and supply must meet demand.

Finding room for international football is difficult given the bloated club season but the possibilities of regular Tonga-Samoa matches feel endless, not just regarding what can happen but where it can happen.

This is a show that can play on the road — it electrifies not just in the old strongholds of Sydney, Brisbane and Auckland or new enclaves like Melbourne, but far beyond.

This game can go to so many places because it can go anywhere the Pasifika diaspora has found itself and, if rugby league wants a way into America that's more than Aussies heading over for the punt and the piss, this is it.

Samoa and Tonga's rivalry turns fans into heroes Ahead of the latest instalment of their timeless rivalry, a new generation of Samoan and Tongan stars have transformed from fans into the new heroes of their nation.

There were pre-game parades as far afield as Houston, Salt Lake City and San Francisco as the Tongan and Samoa communities bolted speakers and flags to their cars and let the Yanks know what was going down on the far side of the world.

They will do it every time because the depth of love for their people is endless and while both teams have evolved to the point where any game they play is a fair event, when they are together a special kind of alchemy occurs.

For some of the players it is bigger than a grand final, and any time you have that kind of emotional investment in this kind of spectacle at this scale it's a sin if you don't do it all the time.

An annual game would be a start. A three-match series in regular intervals would be better. They are ready to come, so get to building it.

What Samoa and Tonga have together goes beyond this sport. These games are just the newest spin on an old story.

But what a story it is, and rugby league must find a way to tell it as many times as possible.

World.title: Russia opens terrorism case over Ukraine oil refinery attack
World.content:
Russian investigators have opened a criminal case on terrorism charges over a Ukrainian attack on an industrial facility in the Nizhny Novgorod region, state news agency TASS reports.

Earlier on Sunday, the region's governor said an unnamed facility had sustained "significant damage" after a "massive" drone attack.

Ukrainian media reported the attack had hit the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it "one of Russia's largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants".

Regional authorities said they were taking all necessary measures to ensure fuel remained available at petrol stations. There were no casualties reported.

Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of households in Ukraine were left without power on Sunday after Russia hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram.

"The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors," Mr Zelenskyy said.

He said Ukraine had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia's Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacturing of Russian missiles.

Overall, Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones across Russian regions overnight.

Ukraine's air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since Saturday evening.

Moscow said on Friday that Ukraine had resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries after a "pause" of several days.

Senior Russian official Alexander Novak told a reporter from state TV that Ukraine had resumed attacks on Russian plants, hitting three oil refineries and one gas-chemical complex.

Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure since Moscow began its offensive there in February 2022.

US President Donald Trump had been pressuring Kyiv for weeks to stop such attacks, blaming them for the rising cost of diesel.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously indicated he would resume peace talks with Ukraine and the US.

A Kremlin aide said on Sunday that Mr Putin would answer the phone to Mr Zelenskyy if he called, saying Putin "has never refused talks", state media reported.

The aide added initial negotiations should include only Russia, Ukraine and the US, with other European countries excluded.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Lebanon's team of tradies win in all-time great finish at World Cup
World.content:
Rugby league fans had been salivating over what might transpire at Western Sydney Stadium on November 1 for months.

It was the first fixture of the World Cup to sell out weeks ago.

Everyone was hyping it up as the moment we would see this tournament catch fire and the international men's game ascend to higher levels than ever seen before.

And that all transpired, except it came a game early.

There was a triple header here, the Jillaroos against Wales, followed by Lebanon and France, to whet the appetite before the main event of Tonga and Samoa.

What no-one anticipated was that Lebanon and France, two minnows who were already well out of contention for the semifinals, would dish up what is roundly being called one of the greatest finishes in the international game.

One that has proven that just because this sport does a World Cup a little differently from the rest, it doesn't diminish its meaning.

Tradies' time to shine

The vast majority of players spread through the teams in this tournament were born in Australia or New Zealand, choosing to represent the country of their heritage.

The French are a rare exception, and after humbling defeats in their first two pool games, they were the underdogs against a Lebanese squad almost entirely consisting of Australian-born players.

But this was no mismatch.

Trailing by two late, France was denied a match-winning try when Lebanon just grounded the ball in the in-goal.

France's Arthur Mourgue then kicked a two-point field goal to send it to golden point shortly after, and in the first period of extra time, Cesar Rouge slotted a one-pointer.

The scenes were beautiful, joyous, crushing, devastating, a chaotic melting pot of emotions savoured by the growing crowd of largely Tongan and Samoan fans.

But it was disallowed for an escort. And so it went on.

The Cedars' Alex Conti missed a long-range penalty goal, which was collected by Mourgue.

He should've held onto it. A more experienced player under this sort of pressure would've taken the tackle, and the quick breather.

But he went for glory, a chip and chase that could've been his crowning glory.

Instead it became his never-ending nightmare.

Abbas Miski gleefully grabbed the goodies, and strolled the short distance to unleash mayhem unlike anything else we've seen at this tournament so far.

Abbas Miski is chaired by teammates after scoring the winning try. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Most of the 30,000 tickets for this game were snapped up by Tongan and Samoan fans.

But a healthy contingent of Sydney's huge Lebanese diaspora turned up, and they were in a heady delirium, as the players danced dazed but delighted, alongside Lebanese drummers on the sidelines.

"It was the saddest I've been this whole tournament and then the happiest I've been this whole tournament. I don't even know what to feel," Lebanon captain Alex Twal told Channel 7.

"We've got plumbers, electricians, foreman, builders … these blokes came here just to have a crack and they're playing against some of the best in the world.

"Abbas, he's a winger, he's never played back row. For him to come up with a play like that, it's true Lebanese spirit.

"I've got goosebumps. I love being Lebanese."

Loading Instagram content

Twal was born a stone's throw from this stadium at Westmead. He played his junior footy for the Parramatta City Titans and his entire NRL career has been with Wests Tigers.

Born and raised in Australia, he has a Jordanian father and Lebanese mother.

It is a story similar for so many children of migrants in Australia. An identity that is multidimensional, not having to remain in one neat box, but able to feel connection to many places, roots spread near and far.

Lebanese drummers accompanied hundreds of fans marching to the stadium before the game. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

Lebanese flags flew proudly outside the stadium ahead of the game. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

And so often sport is the powerful vehicle that helps drive that message home.

That is why even though this game was a dead rubber, a result that ostensibly wouldn't change the world, it still meant something more than footy.

Because for people who have sometimes felt like they're between worlds, between cultures, there is somewhere they belong.

The hundreds of Lebanese fans who sang and marched to the beat of their traditional drums to the stadium today felt it, and no doubt many more in Australia's sizeable Lebanese community.

This may be the end of the line for the Cedars, in the short term at least.

They are ineligible for future tournaments having been downgraded to an affiliate member by the International Rugby League.

Meaning, for now, their greatest World Cup moment may very well be their last.

And the French must take heart from showing fight till the very end.

They were a team always up against it when facing players who have had league in their blood from birth.

And there will be hope they can try to inspire some sort of renaissance in the sport in the Northern Hemisphere, where it is currently on life support.

But rising from the ashes is what rugby league does best.

World.title: Mine rescue teams compete underground in biggest competition in a decade
World.content:
Emergency response teams tasked with keeping miners safe in one of the most complex working environments on the planet have put themselves to the test in Western Australia's annual Underground Mine Rescue Competition.

Fire casualty Jade Doyle is an ERT volunteer who could not compete this year but still wanted to be part of the event. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

While the equipment has changed, the volunteer ethos draws on more than 100 years of emergency response traditions across WA's mining industry.

Mine emergency response teams (ERT) train in everything from firefighting to underwater rescue to first aid.

Firefighting was part of the competition for emergency response teams. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Once a year, teams from some of the state's biggest mines gather to test their skills at the competition, run by WA's Chamber of Minerals and Energy.

This year's event brought together 14 teams, the largest field in a decade, to the Gordon Sirdar gold mine, north-east of Kalgoorlie-Boulder and around 630km from Perth.

Teams are scored across a number of categories, both to find the overall winner but also to improve their skills before a real emergency strikes. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

First time for everything

The rescue team from Liontown Resources was competing for the first time, reflecting the lithium miner's status as a relative newcomer in the historic mining region.

Volunteers are dressed in elaborate makeup and had scripts designed to push rescuers to their limits and see if they can remember their training in chaos. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Team captain Meghan Page, a mining engineer, joined the company's rescue team for the opportunity to get "hands-on", and quickly fell in love with it.

"I definitely love ropes the most," she said.

"I am actually slightly afraid of heights, but when I'm on ropes, that all goes away."

Events simulate numerous casualty events, with volunteers dressing up and acting to simulate real situations. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Ms Page said a major reason she joined was knowing there were people watching each other's backs.

"If I had family or a partner on site, I'd want to know that there were people like me and my team training and there if things went wrong," she said.

Hundreds of volunteers took part in the event. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Real-world inspired events

Judges decide the overall winner from points scored from a range of categories, but the main focus remains on preparation for real-world emergencies.

Underground events include real fire and flooded tunnels; even the fake casualties use convincing makeup to make it feel real.

Mines Rescue Committee chair Daniel Goss, a 20-year industry veteran, said months of preparation went into the event.

Daniel Goss has been in mine rescue for 20 years and says its hard to estimate how many hundreds or thousands of hours go into setting up mine rescue events. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

"What we do … is create a really realistic, dynamic environment, put the teams under pressure," Mr Goss said.

"[We] put them through fairly intense and developed scenarios to really look at how those skills play out in an actual scenario."

Officials carefully shadow teams noting what they do right and wrong to help them prepare. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

The Varischetti Rescue of March 1907 in WA's remote Goldfields shows just how much the technology has changed, but the risks remain the same.

Modesto "Charlie" Varischetti became trapped underground at the Bonnievale gold mine after a sudden storm saw floodwaters break into the mine's underground tunnels.

Modesto Varischetti was 300 metres underground when floodwater trapped him in an air pocket for nine days. (Supplied: Coolgardie Visitor Centre & Museum)

Four volunteer divers worked for nine days to rescue the mine worker, using the diving equipment of the day to stage a miracle rescue.

The underwater obstacles at this year's event were designed to be similar to conditions during the 2018 Thai cave rescue, and state-of-the-art technology will be made available to teams.

A family tradition

Northern Star Resources' Maritza Potgieter has been part of the mine rescue team for seven years.

"Our family have always been part of working in mining and always been part of the emergency response teams," she said.

" My dad … was a little bit apprehensive of me joining, but as the time went on, I think he was pretty proud. "

Organisers work to make the annual mine rescue competitions as realistic as possible. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

She enjoyed the work so much, she now works as the miner's rescue coordinator.

"The biggest thing for me was … how close you become with the other ERT members," she said.

"I think that's definitely what's drawn me the most to ERT and why I will continue doing it probably for the rest of my life."

Teams from across the Eastern Goldfields attended the competition on Sunday, representing some of the largest miners in the state. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Lessons learned

Attending the underground competition for the first time, Evolution Mining medic Annika Messervy said she joined the ERT team 18 months ago because it frightened her.

Annika Messervy became an ERT because it was something that frightened her and says it makes her stronger every day. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

"I think I've become a much more confident person with it; everyone I've met through it is so wonderful," she said.

"It's been so much fun … it's a fantastic community."

With competitions wrapping up on Sunday, teams attend an awards ceremony before returning home to put what they learned into practice.

World.title: Driver charged after pedestrian's death in Adelaide's north
World.content:
A pedestrian has died, while another was seriously injured, after a crash in Adelaide's northern suburbs on Sunday morning.

SA Police say emergency services were called to the intersection of Waterloo Corner Road and Whites Road in Salisbury North just after 10am when a vehicle collided with a traffic light pole and two pedestrians.

"Sadly, one of the pedestrians died at the scene and the second pedestrian was taken to hospital with serious injuries," a spokesperson said.

The driver was arrested at 11:20am and charged with causing death by dangerous driving and causing serious harm by dangerous driving.

"He was granted bail and will appear in the Elizabeth Magistrates Court on 14 December," they said.

The 19-year-old driver, who was uninjured, was issued with an instant loss of licence until further order.

Police said the crash occurred after 10am on Sunday. (ABC News)

Road closures were in place, and the intersection was closed.

Major crash investigators attended the scene and are examining the surrounding circumstances, while anyone who witnessed or has dashcam footage has been asked to contact police.

The pedestrian's life is the 90th lost on SA roads this year.

World.title: Megan is a Perth public housing tenant. Her neighbours are making her life hell
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAPublic housing Megan is a Perth public housing tenant. Her neighbours are making her life hell Hannah Murphy November 2, 2026 — 2:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Megan* is a public housing tenant in Cloverdale. She came to live at the small, well-kept home after she spent time in a women’s refuge a few years ago, after escaping an abusive relationship. Her home is airy and neat, and she is glowing about the local community. “It’s nice. We have a WhatsApp group … if someone’s parcel gets delivered to the wrong house, you can pop it in there and ask ‘is this yours’?,” she says. “Another time, a neighbour’s dog passed away, so we all had a barbecue down by the river to celebrate their life.



But, she says, her quiet pocket of Cloverdale was upended a few years ago when she got a new neighbour in the public housing block next to hers. Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Debra complained about her Rivervale neighbours 60 times in three years. It’s worse than ever “It just changed the whole atmosphere of the street,” she says. Megan said the problems started almost immediately. Rubbish bins on the street would frequently overflow, and sheets were strung up in the front yard’s carport. Strange men would come to the address at all hours of the day - occasionally knocking on her front door after mixing up the address. Cars were parked out the front of the home with missing licence plates and paint stripped off, and people started doing drugs openly on the street.



Over time, Megan’s neighbours say they have reported the tenants for dealing drugs, breaking in to neighbour’s cars and homes, and even for abusing their own children. Often, those reports had to be directed to WA police. Rubbish on the street from the house. Hannah Murphy “[There’s a] little girl there who has some fair developmental problems,” Megan says. “The abuse [the tenant] is inflicting on her has had me in tears.” She even recalls a time she was standing in her own backyard when a woman at the property thought she overheard Megan gossiping. She attempted to climb the fence, telling Megan she would kill her, causing her to phone the police.



Unfortunately for Brent*, a next door neighbour of Megan’s, he has also had to call the authorities when dealing with the tenants. “It’s deteriorated so badly,” he said. “There are people moving in and out, and we don’t even know who they are … you’ve got four kids living in a two-bedroom house, and they’ve got people coming and going and staying at night. “It’s not healthy. “I’ve got a baby who is two years old. I don’t want them seeing this.”



Inside the car port of a department property. Hannah Murphy Brent says he has phoned the Department of Housing’s disruptive behaviour team about “four or five” times over the years but says he feels he has effectively been discouraged from making an official complaint. He says he was often told to direct his frustrations to police. “It is absolutely frustrating … . they demotivate you in any possible way from even talking to them,” Brent says. He says in his view, the police and the department rarely communicate and as a result, problem tenants are hide to identify. It is an experience shared by Megan, who says she has made similar complaints to the Department of Housing over the years.



“I’ve given up a little bit,” she says. “I just try to make peace. I’ve also got a disability, so the stress of it all is just - to me - too much.” Instead, she has installed security cameras all around her property and when it becomes too bad, she goes away to stay with a friend. She says ultimately, she is concerned other public housing tenants like her are missing out on homes in favour of people like her neighbour. “My best friend - she is a single mum with a baby. If she could have had one of these homes, and she would have cherished it,” Megan says.



Brent agrees. “My old next door neighbour … she is a pensioner and her ceiling collapsed. She has had to move out,” he says. “The [house she is now renting], the rent is so high she can’t even afford to actually feed herself, let alone all the bills and everything. “Some of the neighbours were actually supporting her with a bit of groceries … but she deserves a house.” Brent says he has now decided to move out and sell their family home over the ongoing problem.



Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Footage captures teen allegedly charging man with machete at Perth shops “I wanted to live there my whole life,” he says. “I would like to ask the Minister - would you live next to that sort of neighbour? Would you raise your kids next to this neighbour, where you see antisocial behaviour day in day out, and drugs, and all this actually happening right in front of your house?” Minister John Carey says it is absolutely crucial locals report problems with the department for them to act. “Our government is committed to integrating social and affordable housing across all communities, with a number of large scale build to rent projects underway in my electorate,” he says.



”We are the landlord for some of the most vulnerable in our society, and I expect all tenants to adhere to their obligations and respect their neighbours. “The Department of Housing and Works works closely with tenants and external support agencies to manage tenancy issues and support tenants to sustain their tenancy, where possible. “Complaints must be made to the department’s disruptive behaviour reporting line in order for any disruptive behaviour to be investigated. “Where there is serious or ongoing disruptive behaviour, the department is committed to taking action.” However, Carey highlighted that there are restrictions in the department’s power.



“The decision to evict ultimately sits with the magistrate, who will only grant an order for vacant possession if they are satisfied that there has been a breach of the tenancy agreement, and that the tenant has been given every opportunity to rectify the breach and has failed to do so,” he says. Minister for Housing John Carey. Thomas Wielecki “The department is not a law enforcement agency and any criminal behaviour should be reported to the police.” Which, Brent says, is the problem. *Megan and Brent’s names have been changed to protect them from reprisal.
