World.title: Homes losing $9000 a month as RBA mulls another rate hike
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Homes losing $9000 a month as RBA mulls another rate hike Shane Wright November 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The nationwide slump in house values has spread to Brisbane and Perth with no signs the property downturn is close to ending, amid fears it could get worse if the Reserve Bank pushes ahead with another interest rate hike this week. Figures released today by Cotality show the nation’s property values fell another 1.2 per cent in October, the seventh consecutive monthly drop, to be down 6.7 per cent since March. In dollar terms, median property values have slumped by $63,400 or more than $9000 a month. House values are falling by $9000 a month. Getty Images Sydney’s median house price fell another 1.9 per cent through the month to be down by 11.1 per cent since the start of the year. The median unit price dropped by 0.7 per cent to be down by 6.5 per cent. Melbourne’s median house price edged down by 1 per cent to $906,000. It has fallen by 9 per cent so far this year. The city’s median unit price slipped by 0.3 per cent in October and is down by 4.7 per since the start of 2026.



But bigger falls are now being recorded across the country in cities which have had the largest increase in values over recent years. Brisbane’s median house value fell by 2 per cent last month and is now the weakest market in the country with values down by 6.2 per cent over the past three months. Perth’s median house value fell by 1.7 per cent in October, it slipped by 1.2 per cent in Adelaide while it eased 1 per cent in Canberra. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese distances Labor from RBA, calls rate hikes a ‘blunt instrument’ In April, the median house price was above $1 million in five capitals. Sydney’s median, though the highest in the country at $1.6 million, had already been falling for two months, while the other capitals in the $1 million club were Brisbane, Perth, Canberra and Adelaide. Now just Sydney, at $1.44 million, and Brisbane ($1.1 million) are over the $1 million mark.



Cotality research manager Tim Lawless said it was clear the downturn in the property market had stretched across the country. “Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in values over the past three months,” he said. Two markets defied last month’s fall. House values lifted by 0.6 per cent in both Hobart, where the median price is almost $797,000, and in Darwin, where it sits at $745,726. Across every part of Sydney and Melbourne, values are falling. In Sydney, the smallest drop has been in the city’s south-west with values down by 1.4 per cent over the past year in Wollondilly and by 1.6 per cent in Camden. In Melbourne, the smallest annual decline has been in the city centre, down by just 0.3 per cent, while values have eased by 0.7 per cent in the outer north-west around Sunbury.



Outside the capitals, most regional areas are still well up on where they were a year ago. They include WA’s Goldfields region (up 23.8 per cent), the Darling Downs of Queensland (18.2 per cent), Dubbo in NSW (11.7 per cent) and Victoria’s Glenelg region (7.9 per cent). The fall in housing prices is feeding into the rental market. Cotality research director Tim Lawless says property values in cities such as Perth and Brisbane are now falling faster than Sydney or Melbourne. Australian Financial Review Cotality said the national vacancy rate rose to 2.3 per cent, just below its decade-long average of 2.4 per cent and the highest since January 2022, which was the month before the international border was fully re-opened. Vacancy rates were higher than a year ago in every capital city bar Darwin. Cotality also noted that the pace of rental increases is easing, with the 0.9 per cent lift in the past three months the smallest since January 2025.



Lawless said demand-side factors such as those that had affected home values were at play in the rental market. “Renters are likely to be approaching a ceiling on their capacity to pay more, following a 52 per cent surge in rents over the past six years, which added around $245 a week to the median rental rate nationally,” he said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers recently told this masthead’s Inside Politics podcast that while the budget’s tax changes had contributed to the drop in property prices, they were not the only reason for the current downturn. “I think it would be dishonest to say that the tax changes are solely responsible, or that they’re not responsible at all,” he said. Lawless said higher interest rates, the run-up in prices over recent years, cost-of-living pressures and the government’s budget measures had all contributed to the slide in prices.



The pressure on the market is likely to intensify after Tuesday, with financial markets and economists expecting the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy board to deliver its fifth rate hike this year. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver, who expects the bank to take the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, said households were suffering a double whammy from higher mortgage repayments and the surge in petrol prices. He said a quarter percentage point hike on Tuesday would add about $110 to monthly repayments on an average mortgage, taking the increase so far this year to $550 a month or $6600 a year. The lift in petrol prices had added almost $100 a month to monthly petrol bills. “So around a $640-a-month extra impost since January for those with a mortgage and petrol car, which is quite a hit,” he said. World.title: Trust in politicians plunges, new polling shows, as education divide splits Australian voters
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Trust in Australia’s politicians has plunged, fewer than half of voters believe they have a meaningful say in government and almost three-quarters think the country has become more divided over the past year. A sweeping assessment of Australia’s democratic health has also exposed a striking divide between university graduates and those whose education ended at high school, with the former far more satisfied with democracy and confident in the integrity of elections. The 2026 McKinnon Index reveals trust in federal politicians has fallen from 35.9 per cent to just 30.5 per cent in a year, while trust in state and territory politicians has dropped six percentage points to 32.7 per cent. The findings come amid a profound realignment of Australian politics, with Pauline Hanson’s One Nation surging in national opinion polls, the major parties struggling to retain voters and fierce debates over immigration, antisemitism and social cohesion following the December 2025 Bondi massacre. The Index suggests Australians are increasingly losing confidence not in democracy itself, but in the politicians who represent them and their ability to bridge the country’s divisions. Trust in the federal government has slipped from 37.6 per cent to 33.1 per cent, with fewer than one in four Australians expressing high trust in political parties. Confidence that Australians can freely express political opinions has plunged almost 10 percentage points, from 67.9 per cent to 58.1 per cent, while fewer than half believe the political system allows people like them to have a say.



Overall satisfaction with democracy has fallen from 54.5 per cent to 50.7 per cent, although more than three-quarters still believe democracy is preferable to any other system of government. But the national figures conceal a deeper divide along education lines. Just 39.7 per cent of Australians whose education ended at high school are satisfied with democracy, compared with 59 per cent of university graduates. The gap is wider still over elections, with almost three-quarters of graduates confident in election outcomes, compared with fewer than half of Australians with a high school education or below. The findings suggest educational attainment is now a much stronger dividing line than income across several measures of democratic confidence and participation, raising questions about whether Australia’s political institutions are equally accessible to all citizens. The research, based on interviews with 4273 Australians conducted by Roy Morgan between June 19 and July 21, comes amid heightened concern about political hostility following the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines outside her Wangaratta electorate office this month.



McKinnon interim executive chairman John Thwaites - a former Victorian deputy premier - said the findings revealed growing disconnection between Australians and their elected representatives. “People need to know their voice matters,” Thwaites said. “They also need to see leaders acting with integrity, keeping their promises and delivering outcomes that make a difference to their lives. Both matter if we want to rebuild trust.” Editor's pick Analysis

Resolve Political Monitor Chalmers can’t shift any blame on to Trump or Bullock – even if they deserve it Broken promises were cited by 25 per cent, dishonesty by 22.1 per cent and politicians being out of touch by 19 per cent. Another 15.5 per cent nominated self-interest, while just 5.8 per cent cited the cost of living. The deterioration in political confidence has coincided with growing concern about the quality of national debate. More Australians now view political discussion as unhealthy, while 74.4 per cent believe the country has become more divided over the past year.



Political divisions are increasingly spilling into personal relationships, with more than one in five young Australians admitting they would rule out friendships with people who hold different political views. It found 21.8 per cent of men aged 18 to 24 and 21.2 per cent of women in the same age group agreed they could not be friends with someone whose political opinions differed from their own. The intolerance of opposing views was markedly less pronounced among older Australians. Just 4.5 per cent of men and 6.3 per cent of women aged over 65 expressed the same sentiment, compared with 11.1 per cent across the population. The survey also exposed a troubling willingness among younger Australians to contemplate political violence. More than one in four men aged 18 to 24 — 27.5 per cent — agreed that extreme measures such as violence could sometimes be justified to advance a cause they cared about, compared with 16.9 per cent of women the same age and 10.1 per cent of Australians overall.

World.title: Tonga win epic over Samoa, Kangaroos learn World Cup semi-final opponent
World.content:
You heard it before you saw it. Even before Addin Fonua-Blake scored, the crowd told the story: Tonga got one over their Pacific rivals Samoa.

In a classic match at Parramatta’s CommBank Stadium, where the colour and the noise did plenty to breathe life into the World Cup on the eve of the knockouts, Tonga pipped Samoa 20-18 to book a semi-final date with New Zealand next Saturday. Australia, the reigning world champions, will host Samoa 24 hours later on Sunday night at Allianz Stadium.

Amongst the vibrant colours of red and blue, only one nation was left standing in the end as Fonua-Blake gave Tonga the last laugh.

The giant prop barged his way through Spencer Leniu to level up the scores for Tonga. All that was left was for Isaiya Katoa to bang over the conversion - and he didn’t miss the chance to lead Tonga into the semi-finals and set up their date with the Kiwis.

Addin Fonua-Blake smiles ahead of his match-winning try. Getty Images

Despite being outscored four tries to three, Katoa’s boot proved to be the difference between the two sides as the classy halfback slotted all three conversion attempts and a first-half penalty.

In stark contrast, Samoa’s Chanel Harris-Tavita missed three conversions, including one midway through the second-half that forced him off with a hamstring injury, before replacement Ronald Volkman banged over a late conversion after enjoying a late cameo.

Tonga’s Robert Toia was named player of the match. The star centre’s dream year continued as he scored the opening try and ended up flattening his Roosters teammate Leniu, who had a miserable night.

Tonga’s fullback Lehi Hopoate celebrates at full-time. Getty Images

In a tense opening 40 minutes, Samoa took an 8-4 lead into half-time after Brian To’o scored the first of two tries. But Katoa’s conversion and penalty proved important.

After being denied a first-half try by the bunker for dropping the ball over the line, Jojo Fifita made no mistake early in the second half as he ran in a simple try to extend Tonga’s lead.

But Fifita got a case of the fumbles soon after and Samoa seized the momentum.

To’o scored his second in the 50th minute, before Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow finished off a stunning try in the 63rd minute.

Five minutes later Samoa had their fourth try, as Volkman showed great strength to score to give the men in blue the lead. His conversion then put Samoa up by four points.

But Fonua-Blake’s try in the 73rd minute levelled up the score, before Katoa kicked Tonga to a slender lead.

Samoa had one late chance of silencing Tonga once and for all, but winger Sua Fa’alogo put a foot into touch as he dived over to score what he hoped was the match-winning try. It ultimately proved the fatal blow.

World.title: The surge in WFH was expected to trigger a baby boom. New data says otherwise
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalFertility The surge in WFH was expected to trigger a baby boom. New data says otherwise Shane Wright November 1, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian research has cast doubt on claims that couples who work from home are more likely to start families or have extra children. Ahead of new figures that are expected to confirm the nation’s fertility rate at a record low, the analysis by independent think-tank e61 suggests factors outside the greater flexibility offered by working from home is not enough for couples to take the parenthood plunge. Australian research has cast doubt on the claim that working-from-home rules encourage women to have more children. Getty Images Fertility rates around the developed world have been falling for decades, prompting an avalanche of government policies stretching from making mothers with several children tax-free to direct financial handouts. Some analysis has suggested that enabling people to work from home both reduces some costs associated with having children while also making it easier on parents to care for their newborns.



Research released earlier this year by a group of academics from Germany, the United States and Britain found adults who worked from home at least one day a week between 2023 and 2025 experienced a higher fertility rate. They found when both parents work at home at least once a week, total fertility lifts by 0.32 children per woman. But soon-to-be-released work by e61 research manager Pelin Akyol suggests there is barely if any change in fertility rates among Australian women who took up working from home during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Related Article Fertility Cash, WFH, childcare overhaul? If we want Australians to have more babies, everything needs to change Akyol compared post-2020 fertility rates of women aged between 30 and 44 across occupations with the ability to work remotely against 2019 levels. Despite the increase in working from home among this group, there was no discernible change in fertility rates. While there was a small “baby bump” in 2021, Australia’s fertility rate started falling again in 2022 and reached a record low of 1.48 births per woman in 2024.



Akyol said the pandemic had created a natural experiment that allowed her to study the impact of the large lift in working from home that had occurred since 2020. While it had enabled more people to work at home, it had not led to a measurable change in fertility. “Australia’s fertility decline is driven by various factors including the cost of raising children, housing affordability, economic security and the career costs of parenthood,” she said. “Working from home can make some parts of family life easier. It reduces commuting time and gives workers more control over where they work, which may make it easier to combine paid work and care. However, it does not remove the financial and time costs of raising children, and it may not reduce the career costs of parenthood.” Related Article Federal budget Gallagher won’t guarantee Labor will cut more than it spends despite mounting pressure Akyol cautioned that her research did not mean workplace flexibility was unimportant for families or that it could have an impact over a longer period.



“Greater flexibility may still help parents combine work and care, even if it is not enough on its own to change fertility decisions. Workplace flexibility is therefore only one part of the fertility debate,” she said. While working from home surged during and out of the pandemic, it was also accompanied by the largest increase in property prices on record with some capitals recording increases of more than 30 per cent. That has prompted claims that high-priced housing, both in Australia and around the developed world, has contributed to the global drop in fertility. In previous periods of economic upheaval, there have been sharp falls in fertility. Australia’s fertility rate fell by 20 per cent during the first five years of the Great Depression. Akyol found that women who were in jobs that were more able to be done from home reported lower intentions to have children after 2020 and said they were less likely to have more children. But she also found that this pattern had started before the pandemic, suggesting that working from home had done nothing to turn around women’s child-rearing plans. Editor's pick Magazine

Sunday Life The November 1 Edition November 1, 2026



The figures come ahead of the latest report on the number of births from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The report will cover 2025. In 2024, there were 292,000 births recorded across the country with the national population at 27.8 million. A decade earlier, there were 300,000 births in a population that was almost 4 million smaller. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Horror fall on Saturday, procedure on Sunday … Melbourne Cup on Tuesday? Jockey’s bid for miracle ride
World.content:
Melbourne Cup Briefing SportRacingMelbourne Cup Horror fall on Saturday, procedure on Sunday … Melbourne Cup on Tuesday? Jockey’s bid for miracle ride Peter Ryan and Danny Russell Updated November 1, 2026 — 10:24pm ,first published 12:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. In this Melbourne Cup Briefing, your wrap of racing news: Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup.

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager calls for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait.

Trainer Nick Ryan is expected to front a Racing Victoria stewards inquiry on Monday on a charge of possessing syringes containing a synthetic EPO. Danny Russell

Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup. Coffey is booked to partner Ciaron Maher’s lightweight fancy Shockletz in the 3200-metre staying test, but is in a race against the clock to recover from a suspected broken collarbone. Harry Coffey (right) on his way back to the mounting yard. Getty Images Connections said Coffey underwent a small procedure on Sunday and was waiting on his doctor to determine whether his injuries were stable enough to ride.



The 31-year-old father of two took a heavy tumble in the second-last race on Derby Day, sending a shockwave across the Flemington crowd. Racegoers feared for his safety as images on the big screen showed Coffey being catapulted into the air after his mount Pondalowie clipped heels and fell. “He has not been ruled in, he has not been ruled out,” Coffey’s manager Dean Hawkes said of the Cup ride on Sunday. The 2024 Caulfield Cup-winning hoop’s ability to cope with pain was evident after Saturday’s mid-race fall. He pulled himself to his feet and walked back to the mounting yard, cradling his arm, before taking part in a stewards’ inquiry. He was then taken to hospital.



Pondalowie was captured by a clerk of the course in the Flemington straight after the scary incident. The six-year-old mare was cleared of injury by vets. The fall happened at the 500m mark and had officials on high alert, following a horse death during the Caulfield Cup earlier this month. After speaking to Coffey, stewards released a report clearing all riders of any blame. “It was established that when the tempo quickened, Pondalowie, despite the efforts of Coffey, shifted in slightly when laying in, resulting in Pondalowie clipping the heels of Cilacap and falling,” stewards said. Maher and Shockletz’s connections will be anxiously awaiting Coffey’s call in case they need to find a replacement rider for the Cup third favourite.



“We’ll give Harry every opportunity and if he can’t do it we’ll find someone else,” Maher said at the Melbourne Cup barrier draw. “It’s a legitimate chance, so anybody would be disappointed if they were riding that horse and they weren’t able to [through injury].” Lightweight jockey Michael Dee has put his hand up for the Shockletz gig if Coffey is ruled out. He gave up his ride on mare Strictly Business, which will be ridden by Dean Yendall.



‘I don’t feel that’s good enough’: International crack at Melbourne Cup technology Peter Ryan

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. The stewards had to make the decision three days out from the race due to the need to lock in the field of 24 at 4.30pm on Saturday, despite the fact the horse may have made the necessary improvement in the remaining two days to take his place. Kevin Blake (left) suggested the technology used for the Melbourne Cup needed to be updated. Getty Images Emergencies are considered impossible because betting technology can’t handle late inclusions to a field of 24.



It means if there are late scratchings between 4.30pm Saturday and the race start, fewer runners will race rather than the next qualified horses in the order of entry being granted a start. Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Racing dodges another nightmare after mid-race fall; Derby Day trainer charged by stewards “We know it’s rigorous, we know it’s tough, and so we’re not going to cry about [the decision]. We’re all big boys and girls, but probably the main takeaway from it is they probably need to sort out their emergency situation,” Blake said. “I’m a guest here so I don’t want to be telling people what to do, but for the reason to be that the technology can’t cope with more than 24 runners in 2026 … I don’t feel that’s good enough.” Defiantly’s withdrawal gives stablemate Kizlyar a start, meaning the O’Brien stable still has five runners – but it robs the race of a natural leader, with the four-year-old gelding a noted frontrunner.



Blake said the jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle, who had been booked to ride Defiantly, would now jump on Sons And Lovers, who was the best drawn of their five starters with barrier three. He said local jockeys James McDonald and Craig Williams would need to weave some magic to their mounts Trustyourinstinct and James J Braddock in a good spot after they drew barriers 18 and 24 respectively. Related Melbourne Cup Pick your winners with our 2026 Melbourne Cup sweep McDonald is the in-form jockey after an exhilarating Derby Day where he won four races including the Derby and Trustyourinstinct is sure to win support due to his presence in the saddle. “James is going to have to work his magic to get in and get cover [and] get him racing efficiently, but he is a very classy horse unexposed to the trip,” Blake said.



“[He] looks to have a leading chance in the book, so you just hope he gets a kind spin from the draw.” Last year’s runner-up Goodie Two Shoes is said to be in better form than last season and is expected to carry big bets from his owner J.P. McManus. Blake also talked up Kizlyar’s chances despite his disappointing run in the Moonee Valley Cup, which became a sit and sprint at the finish. Defiantly may run in the Queen Elizabeth Stakes on Saturday as a consolation, with O’Brien due to fly in from the Breeders’ Cup, which is raced in the US, on Monday. Meanwhile at Werribee, Ethan Brown was pleased with Point of Law’s work on Sunday when he visited the horse he rode to victory in the Geelong Cup.



Ryan to front stewards inquiry Danny Russell

Trainer Nick Ryan is expected to front a Racing Victoria stewards inquiry on Monday on a charge of possessing syringes containing a synthetic EPO. Stewards raided Ryan’s Flemington stables on Derby Day morning and allegedly found syringes in the glove box of his car containing Darbepoetin Alfa – a man-made stimulating agent that mimics a natural hormone. Darbepoetin Alfa is listed as a prohibited substance under the rules of racing. As a result, Ryan’s two runners on Derby Day – Doubt Time and Anglais – were scratched. Stewards will seek further evidence from the former jockey at Monday’s hearing after he reserved his plea on Saturday. The hearing will be closed.

World.title: Freo turn to Wharfie Time in the AFLW … but fail to score; All-Victorian top four locked in
World.content:
Sydney have confirmed their home AFLW elimination final against the Western Bulldogs after overcoming Wharfie Time and a horror injury to beat Fremantle by one point.

Play was held up for 10 minutes in the first quarter on Sunday at Cockburn before Swans ruck Caitlin Reid was stretchered from the field. She was felled by a clash of heads with Fremantle’s Hayley Miller.

After Sydney rallied in the second half and took the lead, Miller snapped a goal to bring the Dockers to within one point and Wharfie Time was sounded, with less than 90 seconds on the clock.

But just as the crowd activation backfired horribly in the AFL grand final loss to Brisbane, the Dockers could not score again.

Chloe Molloy took a game-saving mark with 15 seconds left and the Swans won 5.7 (37) to 5.6 (36), denying Dockers star Ash Brazill a farewell win.

Molloy kicked four goals to break the AFLW goalkicking record with 28, two up on Hawthorn’s Aine McDonagh and Geelong forward Jackie Perry. Sydney racked up nine wins, a club record.

“It’s a good catapult ... into the finals, close wins like that,” Molloy told Fox Footy.

“It always brings out a bit extra energy, especially when you hear Wharfie Time.”

Geelong will host Melbourne, followed by reigning premiers North Melbourne against Carlton in a qualifying-final double header next Saturday afternoon at Ikon Park.

Sydney expect to pack out Henson Park on Sunday against the Bulldogs, before Gold Coast host Hawthorn in the other elimination final.

World.title: Megan is a Perth public housing tenant. Her neighbours are making her life hell
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAPublic housing Megan is a Perth public housing tenant. Her neighbours are making her life hell Hannah Murphy November 2, 2026 — 2:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Megan* is a public housing tenant in Cloverdale. She came to live at the small, well-kept home after she spent time in a women’s refuge a few years ago, after escaping an abusive relationship. Her home is airy and neat, and she is glowing about the local community. “It’s nice. We have a WhatsApp group … if someone’s parcel gets delivered to the wrong house, you can pop it in there and ask ‘is this yours’?,” she says. “Another time, a neighbour’s dog passed away, so we all had a barbecue down by the river to celebrate their life.



But, she says, her quiet pocket of Cloverdale was upended a few years ago when she got a new neighbour in the public housing block next to hers. Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Debra complained about her Rivervale neighbours 60 times in three years. It’s worse than ever “It just changed the whole atmosphere of the street,” she says. Megan said the problems started almost immediately. Rubbish bins on the street would frequently overflow, and sheets were strung up in the front yard’s carport. Strange men would come to the address at all hours of the day - occasionally knocking on her front door after mixing up the address. Cars were parked out the front of the home with missing licence plates and paint stripped off, and people started doing drugs openly on the street.



Over time, Megan’s neighbours say they have reported the tenants for dealing drugs, breaking in to neighbour’s cars and homes, and even for abusing their own children. Often, those reports had to be directed to WA police. Rubbish on the street from the house. Hannah Murphy “[There’s a] little girl there who has some fair developmental problems,” Megan says. “The abuse [the tenant] is inflicting on her has had me in tears.” She even recalls a time she was standing in her own backyard when a woman at the property thought she overheard Megan gossiping. She attempted to climb the fence, telling Megan she would kill her, causing her to phone the police.



Unfortunately for Brent*, a next door neighbour of Megan’s, he has also had to call the authorities when dealing with the tenants. “It’s deteriorated so badly,” he said. “There are people moving in and out, and we don’t even know who they are … you’ve got four kids living in a two-bedroom house, and they’ve got people coming and going and staying at night. “It’s not healthy. “I’ve got a baby who is two years old. I don’t want them seeing this.”



Inside the car port of a department property. Hannah Murphy Brent says he has phoned the Department of Housing’s disruptive behaviour team about “four or five” times over the years but says he feels he has effectively been discouraged from making an official complaint. He says he was often told to direct his frustrations to police. “It is absolutely frustrating … . they demotivate you in any possible way from even talking to them,” Brent says. He says in his view, the police and the department rarely communicate and as a result, problem tenants are hide to identify. It is an experience shared by Megan, who says she has made similar complaints to the Department of Housing over the years.



“I’ve given up a little bit,” she says. “I just try to make peace. I’ve also got a disability, so the stress of it all is just - to me - too much.” Instead, she has installed security cameras all around her property and when it becomes too bad, she goes away to stay with a friend. She says ultimately, she is concerned other public housing tenants like her are missing out on homes in favour of people like her neighbour. “My best friend - she is a single mum with a baby. If she could have had one of these homes, and she would have cherished it,” Megan says.



Brent agrees. “My old next door neighbour … she is a pensioner and her ceiling collapsed. She has had to move out,” he says. “The [house she is now renting], the rent is so high she can’t even afford to actually feed herself, let alone all the bills and everything. “Some of the neighbours were actually supporting her with a bit of groceries … but she deserves a house.” Brent says he has now decided to move out and sell their family home over the ongoing problem.



Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Footage captures teen allegedly charging man with machete at Perth shops “I wanted to live there my whole life,” he says. “I would like to ask the Minister - would you live next to that sort of neighbour? Would you raise your kids next to this neighbour, where you see antisocial behaviour day in day out, and drugs, and all this actually happening right in front of your house?” Minister John Carey says it is absolutely crucial locals report problems with the department for them to act. “Our government is committed to integrating social and affordable housing across all communities, with a number of large scale build to rent projects underway in my electorate,” he says.



”We are the landlord for some of the most vulnerable in our society, and I expect all tenants to adhere to their obligations and respect their neighbours. “The Department of Housing and Works works closely with tenants and external support agencies to manage tenancy issues and support tenants to sustain their tenancy, where possible. “Complaints must be made to the department’s disruptive behaviour reporting line in order for any disruptive behaviour to be investigated. “Where there is serious or ongoing disruptive behaviour, the department is committed to taking action.” However, Carey highlighted that there are restrictions in the department’s power.



“The decision to evict ultimately sits with the magistrate, who will only grant an order for vacant possession if they are satisfied that there has been a breach of the tenancy agreement, and that the tenant has been given every opportunity to rectify the breach and has failed to do so,” he says. Minister for Housing John Carey. Thomas Wielecki “The department is not a law enforcement agency and any criminal behaviour should be reported to the police.” Which, Brent says, is the problem. *Megan and Brent’s names have been changed to protect them from reprisal.

World.title: Homes losing $9000 a month as RBA mulls another rate hike
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Homes losing $9000 a month as RBA mulls another rate hike Shane Wright November 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The nationwide slump in house values has spread to Brisbane and Perth with no signs the property downturn is close to ending, amid fears it could get worse if the Reserve Bank pushes ahead with another interest rate hike this week. Figures released today by Cotality show the nation’s property values fell another 1.2 per cent in October, the seventh consecutive monthly drop, to be down 6.7 per cent since March. In dollar terms, median property values have slumped by $63,400 or more than $9000 a month. House values are falling by $9000 a month. Getty Images Sydney’s median house price fell another 1.9 per cent through the month to be down by 11.1 per cent since the start of the year. The median unit price dropped by 0.7 per cent to be down by 6.5 per cent. Melbourne’s median house price edged down by 1 per cent to $906,000. It has fallen by 9 per cent so far this year. The city’s median unit price slipped by 0.3 per cent in October and is down by 4.7 per since the start of 2026.



But bigger falls are now being recorded across the country in cities which have had the largest increase in values over recent years. Brisbane’s median house value fell by 2 per cent last month and is now the weakest market in the country with values down by 6.2 per cent over the past three months. Perth’s median house value fell by 1.7 per cent in October, it slipped by 1.2 per cent in Adelaide while it eased 1 per cent in Canberra. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese distances Labor from RBA, calls rate hikes a ‘blunt instrument’ In April, the median house price was above $1 million in five capitals. Sydney’s median, though the highest in the country at $1.6 million, had already been falling for two months, while the other capitals in the $1 million club were Brisbane, Perth, Canberra and Adelaide. Now just Sydney, at $1.44 million, and Brisbane ($1.1 million) are over the $1 million mark.



Cotality research manager Tim Lawless said it was clear the downturn in the property market had stretched across the country. “Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in values over the past three months,” he said. Two markets defied last month’s fall. House values lifted by 0.6 per cent in both Hobart, where the median price is almost $797,000, and in Darwin, where it sits at $745,726. Across every part of Sydney and Melbourne, values are falling. In Sydney, the smallest drop has been in the city’s south-west with values down by 1.4 per cent over the past year in Wollondilly and by 1.6 per cent in Camden. In Melbourne, the smallest annual decline has been in the city centre, down by just 0.3 per cent, while values have eased by 0.7 per cent in the outer north-west around Sunbury.



Outside the capitals, most regional areas are still well up on where they were a year ago. They include WA’s Goldfields region (up 23.8 per cent), the Darling Downs of Queensland (18.2 per cent), Dubbo in NSW (11.7 per cent) and Victoria’s Glenelg region (7.9 per cent). The fall in housing prices is feeding into the rental market. Cotality research director Tim Lawless says property values in cities such as Perth and Brisbane are now falling faster than Sydney or Melbourne. Australian Financial Review Cotality said the national vacancy rate rose to 2.3 per cent, just below its decade-long average of 2.4 per cent and the highest since January 2022, which was the month before the international border was fully re-opened. Vacancy rates were higher than a year ago in every capital city bar Darwin. Cotality also noted that the pace of rental increases is easing, with the 0.9 per cent lift in the past three months the smallest since January 2025.



Lawless said demand-side factors such as those that had affected home values were at play in the rental market. “Renters are likely to be approaching a ceiling on their capacity to pay more, following a 52 per cent surge in rents over the past six years, which added around $245 a week to the median rental rate nationally,” he said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers recently told this masthead’s Inside Politics podcast that while the budget’s tax changes had contributed to the drop in property prices, they were not the only reason for the current downturn. “I think it would be dishonest to say that the tax changes are solely responsible, or that they’re not responsible at all,” he said. Lawless said higher interest rates, the run-up in prices over recent years, cost-of-living pressures and the government’s budget measures had all contributed to the slide in prices.



The pressure on the market is likely to intensify after Tuesday, with financial markets and economists expecting the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy board to deliver its fifth rate hike this year. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver, who expects the bank to take the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, said households were suffering a double whammy from higher mortgage repayments and the surge in petrol prices. He said a quarter percentage point hike on Tuesday would add about $110 to monthly repayments on an average mortgage, taking the increase so far this year to $550 a month or $6600 a year. The lift in petrol prices had added almost $100 a month to monthly petrol bills. “So around a $640-a-month extra impost since January for those with a mortgage and petrol car, which is quite a hit,” he said. World.title: Trust in politicians plunges, new polling shows, as education divide splits Australian voters
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Trust in Australia’s politicians has plunged, fewer than half of voters believe they have a meaningful say in government and almost three-quarters think the country has become more divided over the past year. A sweeping assessment of Australia’s democratic health has also exposed a striking divide between university graduates and those whose education ended at high school, with the former far more satisfied with democracy and confident in the integrity of elections. The 2026 McKinnon Index reveals trust in federal politicians has fallen from 35.9 per cent to just 30.5 per cent in a year, while trust in state and territory politicians has dropped six percentage points to 32.7 per cent. The findings come amid a profound realignment of Australian politics, with Pauline Hanson’s One Nation surging in national opinion polls, the major parties struggling to retain voters and fierce debates over immigration, antisemitism and social cohesion following the December 2025 Bondi massacre. The Index suggests Australians are increasingly losing confidence not in democracy itself, but in the politicians who represent them and their ability to bridge the country’s divisions. Trust in the federal government has slipped from 37.6 per cent to 33.1 per cent, with fewer than one in four Australians expressing high trust in political parties. Confidence that Australians can freely express political opinions has plunged almost 10 percentage points, from 67.9 per cent to 58.1 per cent, while fewer than half believe the political system allows people like them to have a say.



Overall satisfaction with democracy has fallen from 54.5 per cent to 50.7 per cent, although more than three-quarters still believe democracy is preferable to any other system of government. But the national figures conceal a deeper divide along education lines. Just 39.7 per cent of Australians whose education ended at high school are satisfied with democracy, compared with 59 per cent of university graduates. The gap is wider still over elections, with almost three-quarters of graduates confident in election outcomes, compared with fewer than half of Australians with a high school education or below. The findings suggest educational attainment is now a much stronger dividing line than income across several measures of democratic confidence and participation, raising questions about whether Australia’s political institutions are equally accessible to all citizens. The research, based on interviews with 4273 Australians conducted by Roy Morgan between June 19 and July 21, comes amid heightened concern about political hostility following the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines outside her Wangaratta electorate office this month.



McKinnon interim executive chairman John Thwaites - a former Victorian deputy premier - said the findings revealed growing disconnection between Australians and their elected representatives. “People need to know their voice matters,” Thwaites said. “They also need to see leaders acting with integrity, keeping their promises and delivering outcomes that make a difference to their lives. Both matter if we want to rebuild trust.” Editor's pick Analysis

Resolve Political Monitor Chalmers can’t shift any blame on to Trump or Bullock – even if they deserve it Broken promises were cited by 25 per cent, dishonesty by 22.1 per cent and politicians being out of touch by 19 per cent. Another 15.5 per cent nominated self-interest, while just 5.8 per cent cited the cost of living. The deterioration in political confidence has coincided with growing concern about the quality of national debate. More Australians now view political discussion as unhealthy, while 74.4 per cent believe the country has become more divided over the past year.



Political divisions are increasingly spilling into personal relationships, with more than one in five young Australians admitting they would rule out friendships with people who hold different political views. It found 21.8 per cent of men aged 18 to 24 and 21.2 per cent of women in the same age group agreed they could not be friends with someone whose political opinions differed from their own. The intolerance of opposing views was markedly less pronounced among older Australians. Just 4.5 per cent of men and 6.3 per cent of women aged over 65 expressed the same sentiment, compared with 11.1 per cent across the population. The survey also exposed a troubling willingness among younger Australians to contemplate political violence. More than one in four men aged 18 to 24 — 27.5 per cent — agreed that extreme measures such as violence could sometimes be justified to advance a cause they cared about, compared with 16.9 per cent of women the same age and 10.1 per cent of Australians overall.

World.title: Tonga win epic over Samoa, Kangaroos learn World Cup semi-final opponent
World.content:
You heard it before you saw it. Even before Addin Fonua-Blake scored, the crowd told the story: Tonga got one over their Pacific rivals Samoa.

In a classic match at Parramatta’s CommBank Stadium, where the colour and the noise did plenty to breathe life into the World Cup on the eve of the knockouts, Tonga pipped Samoa 20-18 to book a semi-final date with New Zealand next Saturday. Australia, the reigning world champions, will host Samoa 24 hours later on Sunday night at Allianz Stadium.

Amongst the vibrant colours of red and blue, only one nation was left standing in the end as Fonua-Blake gave Tonga the last laugh.

The giant prop barged his way through Spencer Leniu to level up the scores for Tonga. All that was left was for Isaiya Katoa to bang over the conversion - and he didn’t miss the chance to lead Tonga into the semi-finals and set up their date with the Kiwis.

Addin Fonua-Blake smiles ahead of his match-winning try. Getty Images

Despite being outscored four tries to three, Katoa’s boot proved to be the difference between the two sides as the classy halfback slotted all three conversion attempts and a first-half penalty.

In stark contrast, Samoa’s Chanel Harris-Tavita missed three conversions, including one midway through the second-half that forced him off with a hamstring injury, before replacement Ronald Volkman banged over a late conversion after enjoying a late cameo.

Tonga’s Robert Toia was named player of the match. The star centre’s dream year continued as he scored the opening try and ended up flattening his Roosters teammate Leniu, who had a miserable night.

Tonga’s fullback Lehi Hopoate celebrates at full-time. Getty Images

In a tense opening 40 minutes, Samoa took an 8-4 lead into half-time after Brian To’o scored the first of two tries. But Katoa’s conversion and penalty proved important.

After being denied a first-half try by the bunker for dropping the ball over the line, Jojo Fifita made no mistake early in the second half as he ran in a simple try to extend Tonga’s lead.

But Fifita got a case of the fumbles soon after and Samoa seized the momentum.

To’o scored his second in the 50th minute, before Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow finished off a stunning try in the 63rd minute.

Five minutes later Samoa had their fourth try, as Volkman showed great strength to score to give the men in blue the lead. His conversion then put Samoa up by four points.

But Fonua-Blake’s try in the 73rd minute levelled up the score, before Katoa kicked Tonga to a slender lead.

Samoa had one late chance of silencing Tonga once and for all, but winger Sua Fa’alogo put a foot into touch as he dived over to score what he hoped was the match-winning try. It ultimately proved the fatal blow.

World.title: The surge in WFH was expected to trigger a baby boom. New data says otherwise
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalFertility The surge in WFH was expected to trigger a baby boom. New data says otherwise Shane Wright November 1, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian research has cast doubt on claims that couples who work from home are more likely to start families or have extra children. Ahead of new figures that are expected to confirm the nation’s fertility rate at a record low, the analysis by independent think-tank e61 suggests factors outside the greater flexibility offered by working from home is not enough for couples to take the parenthood plunge. Australian research has cast doubt on the claim that working-from-home rules encourage women to have more children. Getty Images Fertility rates around the developed world have been falling for decades, prompting an avalanche of government policies stretching from making mothers with several children tax-free to direct financial handouts. Some analysis has suggested that enabling people to work from home both reduces some costs associated with having children while also making it easier on parents to care for their newborns.



Research released earlier this year by a group of academics from Germany, the United States and Britain found adults who worked from home at least one day a week between 2023 and 2025 experienced a higher fertility rate. They found when both parents work at home at least once a week, total fertility lifts by 0.32 children per woman. But soon-to-be-released work by e61 research manager Pelin Akyol suggests there is barely if any change in fertility rates among Australian women who took up working from home during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Related Article Fertility Cash, WFH, childcare overhaul? If we want Australians to have more babies, everything needs to change Akyol compared post-2020 fertility rates of women aged between 30 and 44 across occupations with the ability to work remotely against 2019 levels. Despite the increase in working from home among this group, there was no discernible change in fertility rates. While there was a small “baby bump” in 2021, Australia’s fertility rate started falling again in 2022 and reached a record low of 1.48 births per woman in 2024.



Akyol said the pandemic had created a natural experiment that allowed her to study the impact of the large lift in working from home that had occurred since 2020. While it had enabled more people to work at home, it had not led to a measurable change in fertility. “Australia’s fertility decline is driven by various factors including the cost of raising children, housing affordability, economic security and the career costs of parenthood,” she said. “Working from home can make some parts of family life easier. It reduces commuting time and gives workers more control over where they work, which may make it easier to combine paid work and care. However, it does not remove the financial and time costs of raising children, and it may not reduce the career costs of parenthood.” Related Article Federal budget Gallagher won’t guarantee Labor will cut more than it spends despite mounting pressure Akyol cautioned that her research did not mean workplace flexibility was unimportant for families or that it could have an impact over a longer period.



“Greater flexibility may still help parents combine work and care, even if it is not enough on its own to change fertility decisions. Workplace flexibility is therefore only one part of the fertility debate,” she said. While working from home surged during and out of the pandemic, it was also accompanied by the largest increase in property prices on record with some capitals recording increases of more than 30 per cent. That has prompted claims that high-priced housing, both in Australia and around the developed world, has contributed to the global drop in fertility. In previous periods of economic upheaval, there have been sharp falls in fertility. Australia’s fertility rate fell by 20 per cent during the first five years of the Great Depression. Akyol found that women who were in jobs that were more able to be done from home reported lower intentions to have children after 2020 and said they were less likely to have more children. But she also found that this pattern had started before the pandemic, suggesting that working from home had done nothing to turn around women’s child-rearing plans. Editor's pick Magazine

Sunday Life The November 1 Edition November 1, 2026



The figures come ahead of the latest report on the number of births from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The report will cover 2025. In 2024, there were 292,000 births recorded across the country with the national population at 27.8 million. A decade earlier, there were 300,000 births in a population that was almost 4 million smaller. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. In this Melbourne Cup Briefing, your wrap of racing news: Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup.

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager calls for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait.

Trainer Nick Ryan is expected to front a Racing Victoria stewards inquiry on Monday on a charge of possessing syringes containing a synthetic EPO. Danny Russell

Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup. Coffey is booked to partner Ciaron Maher’s lightweight fancy Shockletz in the 3200-metre staying test, but is in a race against the clock to recover from a suspected broken collarbone. Harry Coffey (right) on his way back to the mounting yard. Getty Images Connections said Coffey underwent a small procedure on Sunday and was waiting on his doctor to determine whether his injuries were stable enough to ride.



The 31-year-old father of two took a heavy tumble in the second-last race on Derby Day, sending a shockwave across the Flemington crowd. Racegoers feared for his safety as images on the big screen showed Coffey being catapulted into the air after his mount Pondalowie clipped heels and fell. “He has not been ruled in, he has not been ruled out,” Coffey’s manager Dean Hawkes said of the Cup ride on Sunday. The 2024 Caulfield Cup-winning hoop’s ability to cope with pain was evident after Saturday’s mid-race fall. He pulled himself to his feet and walked back to the mounting yard, cradling his arm, before taking part in a stewards’ inquiry. He was then taken to hospital.



Pondalowie was captured by a clerk of the course in the Flemington straight after the scary incident. The six-year-old mare was cleared of injury by vets. The fall happened at the 500m mark and had officials on high alert, following a horse death during the Caulfield Cup earlier this month. After speaking to Coffey, stewards released a report clearing all riders of any blame. “It was established that when the tempo quickened, Pondalowie, despite the efforts of Coffey, shifted in slightly when laying in, resulting in Pondalowie clipping the heels of Cilacap and falling,” stewards said. Maher and Shockletz’s connections will be anxiously awaiting Coffey’s call in case they need to find a replacement rider for the Cup third favourite.



“We’ll give Harry every opportunity and if he can’t do it we’ll find someone else,” Maher said at the Melbourne Cup barrier draw. “It’s a legitimate chance, so anybody would be disappointed if they were riding that horse and they weren’t able to [through injury].” Lightweight jockey Michael Dee has put his hand up for the Shockletz gig if Coffey is ruled out. He gave up his ride on mare Strictly Business, which will be ridden by Dean Yendall.



‘I don’t feel that’s good enough’: International crack at Melbourne Cup technology Peter Ryan

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. The stewards had to make the decision three days out from the race due to the need to lock in the field of 24 at 4.30pm on Saturday, despite the fact the horse may have made the necessary improvement in the remaining two days to take his place. Kevin Blake (left) suggested the technology used for the Melbourne Cup needed to be updated. Getty Images Emergencies are considered impossible because betting technology can’t handle late inclusions to a field of 24.



It means if there are late scratchings between 4.30pm Saturday and the race start, fewer runners will race rather than the next qualified horses in the order of entry being granted a start. Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Racing dodges another nightmare after mid-race fall; Derby Day trainer charged by stewards “We know it’s rigorous, we know it’s tough, and so we’re not going to cry about [the decision]. We’re all big boys and girls, but probably the main takeaway from it is they probably need to sort out their emergency situation,” Blake said. “I’m a guest here so I don’t want to be telling people what to do, but for the reason to be that the technology can’t cope with more than 24 runners in 2026 … I don’t feel that’s good enough.” Defiantly’s withdrawal gives stablemate Kizlyar a start, meaning the O’Brien stable still has five runners – but it robs the race of a natural leader, with the four-year-old gelding a noted frontrunner.



Blake said the jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle, who had been booked to ride Defiantly, would now jump on Sons And Lovers, who was the best drawn of their five starters with barrier three. He said local jockeys James McDonald and Craig Williams would need to weave some magic to their mounts Trustyourinstinct and James J Braddock in a good spot after they drew barriers 18 and 24 respectively. Related Melbourne Cup Pick your winners with our 2026 Melbourne Cup sweep McDonald is the in-form jockey after an exhilarating Derby Day where he won four races including the Derby and Trustyourinstinct is sure to win support due to his presence in the saddle. “James is going to have to work his magic to get in and get cover [and] get him racing efficiently, but he is a very classy horse unexposed to the trip,” Blake said.



“[He] looks to have a leading chance in the book, so you just hope he gets a kind spin from the draw.” Last year’s runner-up Goodie Two Shoes is said to be in better form than last season and is expected to carry big bets from his owner J.P. McManus. Blake also talked up Kizlyar’s chances despite his disappointing run in the Moonee Valley Cup, which became a sit and sprint at the finish. Defiantly may run in the Queen Elizabeth Stakes on Saturday as a consolation, with O’Brien due to fly in from the Breeders’ Cup, which is raced in the US, on Monday. Meanwhile at Werribee, Ethan Brown was pleased with Point of Law’s work on Sunday when he visited the horse he rode to victory in the Geelong Cup.



Ryan to front stewards inquiry Danny Russell

Trainer Nick Ryan is expected to front a Racing Victoria stewards inquiry on Monday on a charge of possessing syringes containing a synthetic EPO. Stewards raided Ryan’s Flemington stables on Derby Day morning and allegedly found syringes in the glove box of his car containing Darbepoetin Alfa – a man-made stimulating agent that mimics a natural hormone. Darbepoetin Alfa is listed as a prohibited substance under the rules of racing. As a result, Ryan’s two runners on Derby Day – Doubt Time and Anglais – were scratched. Stewards will seek further evidence from the former jockey at Monday’s hearing after he reserved his plea on Saturday. The hearing will be closed.

World.title: Freo turn to Wharfie Time in the AFLW … but fail to score; All-Victorian top four locked in
World.content:
Sydney have confirmed their home AFLW elimination final against the Western Bulldogs after overcoming Wharfie Time and a horror injury to beat Fremantle by one point.

Play was held up for 10 minutes in the first quarter on Sunday at Cockburn before Swans ruck Caitlin Reid was stretchered from the field. She was felled by a clash of heads with Fremantle’s Hayley Miller.

After Sydney rallied in the second half and took the lead, Miller snapped a goal to bring the Dockers to within one point and Wharfie Time was sounded, with less than 90 seconds on the clock.

But just as the crowd activation backfired horribly in the AFL grand final loss to Brisbane, the Dockers could not score again.

Chloe Molloy took a game-saving mark with 15 seconds left and the Swans won 5.7 (37) to 5.6 (36), denying Dockers star Ash Brazill a farewell win.

Molloy kicked four goals to break the AFLW goalkicking record with 28, two up on Hawthorn’s Aine McDonagh and Geelong forward Jackie Perry. Sydney racked up nine wins, a club record.

“It’s a good catapult ... into the finals, close wins like that,” Molloy told Fox Footy.

“It always brings out a bit extra energy, especially when you hear Wharfie Time.”

Geelong will host Melbourne, followed by reigning premiers North Melbourne against Carlton in a qualifying-final double header next Saturday afternoon at Ikon Park.

Sydney expect to pack out Henson Park on Sunday against the Bulldogs, before Gold Coast host Hawthorn in the other elimination final.

AAP

World.title: Police seek help to identify man found in water off Auckland beach
World.content:
Police are asking for help identifying a man whose body was found in the water off an Auckland beach late this afternoon.

Police said emergency services were called to the northern end of Saint Leonards Beach on the North Shore about 5:45pm today after reports that a man's body had been seen in the water.

A member of the public pulled him from the water and CPR was attempted, but the man was pronounced dead on the beach.

Police said he appeared to be of Asian descent, aged 40-50 - possibly in his early 60s.

He is of medium build, has a bald head that may be shaven and no facial hair. He has no obvious marks, scars or tattoos.

The man was not wearing any shoes, but was clad in blue jeans with a bike tyre inner-tube as a belt. He also wore a dark polo shirt with thin light-coloured horizontal stripes, and a pair of blue and green swimming goggles

World.title: 'Space vape' drug warning ahead of summer festival season
World.content:
Drug experts are warning young New Zealanders to be cautious with "space vapes" during the summer festival season.

Space vapes are vape pods containing the drug etomidate, a dissociative anaesthetic drug that the NZ Drug Research Team's Dr Robin van der Sanden said was similar to ketamine.

"It has a legitimate medical use as a general anaesthetic, often for short-term medical procedures, and it produces this powerful but short-acting feeling of euphoria and sedation and physical numbness," she said.

Taking it outside of a medical environment carried risks.

"It's a bit of a volatile compound to take outside of medical supervision. It does often need to be quite precisely dosed, and in a medical operating theatre there'll be someone to check your airways are open and you're breathing properly," she said.

"The risks with vaping etomidate is this unpredictability of how strong the vape pod is and this increased chance for some potentially quite serious negative effects, which range from tremors and muscle spasms through to seizures and a loss of consciousness."

There was a risk the vapes would be shared at parties and festivals, and some New Zealanders might not realise what they were getting into, Dr van der Sanden said.

"The best option would be not to vape an e-liquid that you don't 100 percent know what's in it, or that you haven't purchased yourself. But it would also be good practice to take a small amount first, if you are going to take anything," she said.

Associate professor of criminology at Victoria University Fiona Hutton urged anyone who used space vapes to be upfront with their friends about what might be inside them.

"If you are using an illicit vape at a festival and you're going to be sharing it with other people, you should be really upfront to other people about what you think it contains, and of course what you think it contains may be different to what it actually contains," she said.

World.title: Firefighters bring blaze at South Auckland industrial site under control
World.content:
Firefighters are checking for hotspots after a large blaze at a vehicle parts business in South Auckland.

The fire broke out at Euro Car Parts on Great South Road in Manuwera.

It sent a thick plume of black smoke into the air and sparked phone alerts from Fire and Emergency and Auckland Council.

Firefighters are still putting out a large blaze at a car parts scrap yard in South Auckland.

The fire broke out at Euro Car Parts on Great South Road in Manurewa at about 3:30pm on Sunday.

It sent a thick plume of black smoke into the air and sparked phone alerts from Fire and Emergency and Auckland Council, warning people to avoid the area and for nearby residents to stay indoors.

The smoke from the fire can be seen across South Auckland. NZTA

As of 8pm, the smoke had cleared, and warnings had been lifted.

Fire and Emergency Northern shift manager Garreth Lewis said there were two piles of cars, with the cars stacked on top of each other, which were on fire when crews arrived at the scene.

He said one of the piles was 60 metres high and 60 metres wide, and the cars were stacked too high. He said a second smaller pile was still alight.

World.title: St John moves Levin paramedics to Palmerston North
World.content:
Hato Hone St John has relocated its two extended care paramedics (ECP) from being based in Levin to Palmerston North for a three-month trial.

Its area operations manager for Mid Central, Gareth Collings, said it was intended to make better use of the ECPs' specialist skills across Horowhenua, Manawatū and Tararua, and would not reduce services in Levin, or the number of ECP roles it employed.

It comes amid concerns about care capacity in the region - in September, the last remaining GP at Horowhenua's Taitoko Health clinic resigned, and a former doctor came out of retirement to staff the clinic. And it's left some members of the community concerned about access to care for vulnerable patients.

According to St John's website, ECPs were dispatched by car to patients who could be safely managed in the community, providing a wider range of interventions than standard paramedics - including prescribing short courses of antibiotics, placing urinary catheters, closing wounds and supporting end-of-life care. The model was introduced during the Covid-19 pandemic to better manage less urgent cases outside of hospitals. St John has 46 extended care paramedics nationwide, in Auckland, Hamilton, Levin/Horowhenua, Christchurch, Rangiora, Hokianga and the West Coast.

Now, its two ECPs who previously started and finished their shifts in Levin would instead work from Palmerston North ambulance station, from September until early December. This did not change their ability to respond in Horowhenua, Collings said.

"It allows us to deploy them more effectively to suitable patients with non-life-threatening conditions and complex cases across the wider Mid Central area."

The trial was intended to support greater use of their extended-care capabilities through Hato Hone St John's "patient-centred deployment approach".

"We will monitor the trial closely, including where the ECPs are responding, how effectively their specialist skills are being used and any effect on patient care in Horowhenua and the wider area. No decision about their longer-term base will be made until the trial has been evaluated."

As it was an operational trial, no public consultation was undertaken because it did not remove the service or reduce ECP staffing in Horowhenua.

Lynette Jones, president of the Horowhenua branch of Grey Power, said already the district was finding it difficult to access care.

"The area that we have, it's very wide, very big and of course we've got a lot of people who are elderly," she said.

"We're becoming a bigger population here in Horowhenua, and that has an impact on people getting care when they need it or being looked after when it's an emergency, because there is no emergency department here."

World.title: Police warn league fans after Tauranga convoys
World.content:
Police are urging rugby league fans to consider others, and their own safety, when showing support for their teams.

Hundreds of vehicles took part in convoys backing the Samoan and Tongan sides in Tauranga on Saturday night, prompting complaints about loud stereos, excessive honking and blocked intersections.

"While celebrating cultural heritage and sporting competition is welcomed, it must be done safely and within the law," area prevention manager Inspector Phil Gillbanks said in a statement on Sunday.

Concerns were also raised about unrestrained children and people leaning out vehicle windows.

"Several drivers were stopped and spoken to by police, and infringement notices were issued for offences including operating a vehicle with noisy equipment fitted, permitting or riding in a dangerous position on a vehicle, and failing to wear a seatbelt.

"Police want to make it clear that this type of behaviour will continue to attract enforcement action."

Gillbanks said large flags commonly flown by supporters out vehicle windows could obstruct vision and distract drivers, especially on higher-speed roads.

"Police respect and support the rights of people to celebrate their culture, heritage, and sporting achievements. However, those celebrations must occur in a manner that respects the rights of others, complies with road rules, and does not compromise public safety or disrupt the peace of the community."

Following the convoys, a targeted operation in Mount Maunganui saw more infringements issued.

World.title: Pacific pride takes centre stage as Tonga and Samoa face off
World.content:
The most anticipated pool fixture of the Rugby League World Cup is bringing enormous excitement and unity to South Auckland's Pasifika community.

Tonga XIII and Toa Samoa are going head-to-head on tonight in Sydney, which has been sold out for several weeks, closes the pool play section of the tournament.

The Pacific giants are the last Pacific teams left in the tournament.

There have been car parades in Porirua, with support from local police, to show support for Toa Samoa and Fetu Samoa H0T-Ice CREW & Rahlimatt Auto Services

Dedicated Fans of each team have been showing their love by flying flags proudly from their cars or houses.

For Toa Samoa super fan, Vaovasatoa Paki Scott, he lists three important events in his life, his wedding, the birth of his children and Toa Samoa is also there, but he admits he doesn't want to put them in order, but they are the top three.

While travelling around Auckland, it has been apparent by the countless cars decked out in various flags that the world cup is really bringing out Pacific pride.

And for Sonny Tupou, a Tongan supporter, it's been enjoyable seeing so many different parts of the Pacific represented.

"It's really interesting, there's a Tonga flag, a Samoa flag, Cook Islands and a Niuean. Because we come together because the Pacific Islands is like the community, it's come together as one," he said.

Fans of Tonga have been flying their flags proudly on their vehicles Photo: RNZ / Jessie Chiang

For another Toa Samoa fan, Jame, he said the games have brought his whole family closer together.

"To see my children, they are very proud of who they are and where they come from and to see the community come together, it's great," he said.

Vaovasatoa said this Rugby League World Cup is also bringing to life the dream teams you would normally just speculate about with friends and family after church.

"It's like a video game, it's like I've been able to pick the best of the best and they all want to play for us, and they all want to play represent us, and that's huge for us, we all back them 100 percent."

For Vaovasatoa, Tongan superstar Jason Taumalolo and retired prop Andrew Fifita changed everything in 2017 by choosing Tonga over the Kangaroos and Kiwis respectively.

He said without them, Toa Samoa wouldn't have been able attract NRL stars like Jarome Luai, Stephen Critton or Brian To'o to their ranks.

"We all have to remember, these guys [Taumalolo and Fifita] were at the peak and they choose to play for Tonga, it wasn't at the backend of their career, it wasn't at the very start when we see a lot of our Pacific brothers come back and give back, these guys were right at the top of their game.

Sonny Tupou is not bothered about who wins Sunday's game, because to him the Pacific is all one family.
